utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. We have a long day ahead of us, but I hope fulfilling and productive day and we resume the evidence of Judge Marinkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Marinkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The examination by Mr. Ivetic is not quite complete I understand, so we start with the last part of his examination of you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I ought to be fairly brief today.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Judge Marinkovic, if we could first turn to -- I trust you have the binders back that we had last week that you were working with. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Then for purposes of e-court if we can look at 6D625, and if you could look at that exhibit within the binders that you have. And if you could tell us if you had a personal role in this investigation and what can you tell us about the same.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this document we find a criminal complaint that was submitted by the Pristina SUP. We're looking at the crime of murder committed against Fazlia Murtezi from Pristina. If I look at the substance of this criminal complaint, I see that this occurred on the 13th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In connection with this incident, what I can say is this, I and the other members of the on-site investigation team carried out an on-site investigation that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can move along to 6D -- strike that. 6D338 is on the screen, but while we're waiting for that I can ask you some questions of a preliminary nature. First of all, what do you recall about the killing of Mr. Kelmendi and his sons, was that a matter fully investigated in accord with the applicable laws and rules?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the attachment on the screen in front of me. This was done in keeping with the Law on Criminal Procedure. This is exactly what is done whenever a crime occurs. A criminal complaint was drawn up. There's a record of an on-site investigation, an indictment sent to the Ministry of the Interior, or rather, the organs of the interior for them to take any measure to track down the perpetrator of this crime. And if you look at 6, 7, and 8, what you find is information concerning persons who on that day were found on the site when we conducted our investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now does Exhibit 6D338 reflect all the steps taken in the official investigative process?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Certain steps were possible in terms of being taken by the appropriate state bodies at the time, given the circumstances surrounding this. There was a war on, and no more than that was possible. One thing I can't see in this letter is this, in this specific case when we came across the bodies of these persons, I issued an order for a corpse inspection to be carried out, which is another step that had to be taken under the circumstances, and given the circumstances of the actual on-site investigation. All these were investigative steps that could have been taken by the SUP, the prosecutor, and the investigating magistrate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, could you remind us, please, who Kelmendi was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Bajram Kelmendi was a lawyer based in Pristina. He was one of the better ones. He was exceptionally familiar with criminal law, and I used to work with him during my time in Pristina. Our cooperation was professional and fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Judge Marinkovic, based upon your experiences and work on a daily basis in 1999 during the course of the NATO war, how would you describe the level of cooperation that you witnessed from the Serbian MUP in facilitating on-site investigations and investigating criminal -- and in the work of the investigative judges investigating criminal acts?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my capacity as an investigating judge I cooperated with the bodies of the Ministry of the Interior, and in terms of our on-site investigations the cooperation was very professional and fair. Whenever I issued an order, bodies of the interior would always take all the steps necessary depending on the situation in the circumstances; however, even regardless of the security situation and even regardless of the difficult circumstances that surrounded all of this, whenever a crime occurred I would issue an order and they would do everything to collect any evidence remaining at the crime scene. They would record all of this, draw up files for the prosecutor, themselves, and the appropriate court, and then there would be an order by the public prosecutor for them to proceed and track down any perpetrators. All of this of course was always done in keeping with the Law on Criminal Procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if you could tell us according to the system that was in place in 1998 and 1999, under whose authority fell the detention centres, jails, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The institutions in which any detained persons were kept were under the Ministry of Justice. As for the investigation stage, whenever a detained person wanted to exercise one of their rights, they would go to me because I was the investigating judge, anything that had to do with their status as persons or anything to do with any visits that they were expecting and were allowed to receive.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One moment. I think I have about two questions left for you, ma'am. The first question is: During the course of your work during 1998 and 1999, was there anyone in the Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs that could influences or impact upon your work in any way to control the same, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was independent in my work and professional. No one at all had the power to influence my work. As for how my work was monitored during an investigation, you could tell after an indictment had been issued, if these were criminal proceedings that we're talking about; and then after that, as soon as there was a verdict, this would be sent for verification to a second-instance court which was normally the one in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I think the last question I have for you is during the course of 1998 and 1999, was the work of the investigative judges independent of any other organ, including the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of us who worked for the court were independent and worked on our own. The MUP had no power to influence us or any other state bodies, and other state bodies had any influence over the work of the courts of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Marinkovic. I think you have answered all the questions I have prepared for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Aleksic, do you have questions? No cross-examination by any other Defence counsel. You'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, who in this instance will be Ms. Carter. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Marinkovic.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'd like to start out the cross-examination with just some general information with regards to your background as well as the day-to-day functioning of the court. You had indicated on direct examination that you became a judge in 1984. Can you tell me in 1984 what type of judge were you?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For that let me tell you this, before I became a judge I worked as an associate at the Kosovo Supreme Court in Pristina from 1976 to 1984. I was an associate dealing with administration and litigation concerning administrative issues. When I was appointed judge of the district court in Pristina, I first started dealing with litigations. I started in 1984 and I continued all the way until 1994, when I started working as an investigative judge with that same court.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So you said between 1984 and 1994 you were dealing with litigations. What does that mean? What type of cases were you dealing with and what were your functions?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was mostly about damages, damages of any type, as a result of a traffic accident, for example, or other kinds of damage that were incurred. I dealt with debts, I dealt with property-related issues, I did divorce.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And so you said in 1994 is when you became an investigative judge. Are there different types of investigative judges in the Pristina district court?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the Pristina district court there is only one type of investigative judge, and they deal with all kinds of cases depending on how and where a case is assigned and at what time a case is received.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In the Milosevic case you had testified in regards to the rostering of the investigative judges, that the president of the court makes a schedule, and those in his employ are appointed to criminal cases, civil cases, or an investigative judge. That's what I'm trying to figure out. What type of investigative judges are there or do they handle all types of cases, both criminal and civil?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained on Friday when I started my evidence, I'm not sure if that was recorded or not. Only the president of the court has the power each year when he draws up the yearly schedule, and this is something that is in keeping with the rules --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, I wonder if I could stop you. The question is more specific than that. Are the functions of an investigative judge confined to criminal cases or do you investigate civil cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Investigative judges deal with criminal cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now, once you became an investigative judge, were you able as the district judge rostered each year into the criminal cases, the civil cases, or the investigative judge, were you able to be rostered in any one of those three slots; or once you became an investigative judge you could only be an investigative judge?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was appointed as an investigative judge, I dealt with investigations only. Sometimes I was a member of the first-instance chamber dealing with criminal cases whenever I was not in charge of an investigation, and the president would put me in one of those chambers. Afterwards -- while I worked as an investigating judge I was not involved in trials.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you were appointed to be a criminal investigative judge, what type of training, if any, did you receive to be able to take on those new duties?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No special training is required for that. Whenever I started investigation, I was duty-bound to apply criminal law and the Law on Criminal Procedure, because when you have a trial different kinds of laws are applied.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Dealing with state security cases, there has been an indication by the United Nations report of the Special Rapporteur to the Commission of Human Rights that it was customary for trials involving state security to only be handled in one district and to be brought by one public prosecutor and to be heard by one bench. Is this an accurate picture of what was occurring in Pristina at the time that you were an investigative judge?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies, I didn't receive the first part of the interpretation, which means I'm unable to fully comprehend your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Dealing strictly with state security cases, were they all handled in the Pristina district court?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean when you say "state security cases." I don't think I quite understand that. I'm not sure what you have in mind when referring to state security cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Were terrorism cases held exclusively in the Pristina district court?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Terrorism cases and conspiracy to commit hostile acts were something that was dealt with by all the district courts in -- throughout Kosovo and Metohija because they all had the power to deal with these cases. So it wasn't just the Pristina district court, it was other district courts, too, that dealt with these cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Within the district courts, was there a designated prosecutor who dealt with this type of case?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not really aware of that. There were district prosecutors and deputy district prosecutors. They had a roster and they took up cases as they came. I'm not sure if there was a special prosecutor who was in charge of such cases alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now I want to deal with the make-up of the courts. Is it accurate that out of the 756 judges and prosecutors in Kosovo, that only 30 were actually Kosovar Albanians?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm in no position to confirm the figure for you since I'm not familiar with the exact number of judges and prosecutors in Kosovo and Metohija. I could tell you about the Pristina district court, though. I'm not familiar with any other courts.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In the Pristina district court, how many judges and prosecutors were there?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What period are we looking at? Because the breakdown changed over time, so you'll need to be more specific than that, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: We'll first deal with 1998. In 1998 how many prosecutors and judges within the Pristina district court were there?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was the district prosecutor, all together a total of seven I believe. The judge of the Pristina district court and the president -- I think a total of 19.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How many were Kosovar Albanian?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the court? There were three working with us, three Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In 1999 did those figures change?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the war began we were still all together, but as I mentioned there was one of our colleagues who had died as a result of a heart attack, a stroke. A month later an Albanian colleague of mine who was working an investigation with me left Pristina with his family. So there was one remaining throughout, another Albanian colleague who dealt with second-instance cases, and he was a member of the chamber of the district court.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now I want to move on to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are we clear, these answers, the figure you gave us, three Kosovar Albanians out of 19 related to the judges and the prosecutors taken together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, just the judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We don't have a clear answer, Ms. Carter, if you want to explore the matter further.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You had indicated a figure of 19 persons that were both prosecutors and judges, that was the question that was asked. Does that 19 include prosecutors or is it judges alone?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 19 judges.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How many prosecutors were there?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the Pristina district court there was one and he was a Turk by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: All right. So out of the 19 judges there were three that were Kosovar Albanian, and out of the prosecutors, the single prosecutor, he was a Turk; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: To make sense of that we need to know how many prosecutors there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How many prosecutors were there?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said it a while ago, a total of seven --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You did give us that figure, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now I'd like to move on to the day-to-day functioning. Now, you had indicated that prior to the NATO bombing that you performed on-site investigations upon the direction of the prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but as far as on-site investigations were concerned it was me as an investigating judge who decided whether an on-site investigation should go ahead, and normally this is something I would agree with the prosecutor. But any on-site investigation would fall within my purview because I was an investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: However, prior to the NATO, the only way that an on-site investigation would be started would be at the direction of the prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I could carry out an on-site investigation with or without the prosecutor's consent or approval.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How would a case be referred to you for an on-site investigation that had not come through the prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No application or request was compulsory for an on-site investigation to take place. For example, I happen to be on duty on a Sunday and an incident occurs, there are reasons to suspect that a crime has occurred. I in my capacity as investigating judge am duty-bound to go to the scene of crime to carry out an on-site investigation, and it is the duty team of the Pristina SUP who would be responsible for informing me about any such incidents occurring. They would also have to advise the district public prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So outside of the SUP and the prosecutor, those would be the only two ways that you would be notified of the need for an on-site investigation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would receive notification from the SUP on an incident. As to whether I would go for an on-site investigation or not, this is something I decide on in agreement with the prosecutor. But, for example, a prosecutor can say that they cannot attend the on-site investigation, and in that case I can go ahead alone. It is important that the other team members are present, these being the -- an operational inspector or detective as well as a crime technician, whose attendance is obligatory so that he could take photographs and make sketches. Members of the local police station also have to be present to provide security, and they have to seal off the site itself so as to prevent any unauthorised personnel or people to enter the scene before the arrival of the officials needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now, you just noted that the members of the local police would provide security, and you'd also indicated during direct examination that at times on-site investigations were foregone due to security issues. Did that happen frequently or infrequently, that you had to forego an on-site investigation due to security concerns?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1998 and during the air-strikes, that's when it was happening although not frequently, those were individual cases in which our security was in question and I wasn't able to go there since I was either busy with another on-site investigation or I had hearings or interviews conducted at the court of certain persons involved in investigations. And then the organs of the interior on my authorisation could carry out an on-site investigation without a judge. Also, if we had urgent cases and judges unable to attend for any reason, due to the weather, distance, or security, in such cases more organs of the interior under law were authorised to conduct that piece of investigation on their own and then to further notify both the judge and the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If the MUP was conducting the investigation on their own, was there any limit to the tasks that they were going to be providing?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the on-site investigation they could do the basic things, for example, to search for includes, evidence, and they had to take photographs and sketches with the assistance of the crime technician. They also were obliged to preserve such evidence and hand it over to the authorised judge. The only thing they could not do is issue an order for a corpse inspection and an autopsy to be conducted; only a judge could do that. If there were any witnesses on site or if some persons were found at the site, they could detain them, waiting for an investigative judge. If the judge should not appear, then those people could be taken to see a judge at the court.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any instance in which the MUP had to investigate one of their own, meaning that there was an alleged MUP aggressor and the MUP actually had to investigate one of their own?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, for the record, Your Honour, we did have one last week --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well let -- Mr. Ivetic, let's rely on Mrs. Marinkovic's memory for the moment, and then if necessary you can deal with it in re-examination. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ma'am, can you answer the question, are you aware of any instance in which the MUP had to investigate one of their own, specifically meaning where there was an alleged MUP aggressor and the MUP had to investigate? And specifically -- I'm sorry, one more moment. And specifically that you were not on site, that the MUP had sole freedom to be able to investigate without your overseeing.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An on-site investigation is a part of an investigation into the case. Concerning on-site investigations, the SUP could conduct those on their own. There was a specific example during an air-strike. A criminal complaint was submitted against an unidentified perpetrator, and the court on the public prosecutor's orders continued gathering data so as to identify the perpetrator --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you've misunderstood the question. The question relates to allegations against a member of the MUP. Were there circumstances in which there may be an allegation of murder, for example, against a MUP official where the investigation was carried out by the MUP? That's Ms. Carter's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The MUP itself could not conduct an investigation. They could only gather information and try and identify the perpetrator. They could not undertake an investigation on their own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've just told us that with your authority they could do that where you were engaged somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Concerning on-site investigations, not the investigation as such. An on-site investigation is just an initial phase before an indictment is issued. For that we need to know who the perpetrator is, we have to have reasonable doubt --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Suspicion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and that could only be pursuant to a request made by the competent public prosecutor. We needed to know the crime and the perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, 15, 22, it is getting really confusing because the witness said: Investigation is a phase of the criminal procedure, and the on-site investigation is just a part of it which the investigative judge decides whether or not to undertake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the sense of what you're conveying does emerge from the interpretation that we have. So, Ms. Carter, you'll need to make it clear whether your question relates to on-site investigation or overall investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What types of activities were you allowed to authorise the MUP to conduct? Was this on-site investigations or something more?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning on-site investigations, as a procedure that means that the case has not been initiated yet. The organs of the interior under my authority could conduct an on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, there's a linguistic problem here. You regard I think the conduct of your own investigators, the OTP, as an investigation. I think that the Serb legal system would not regard that as an investigation, that something more formal constitutes an investigation under the Serb system. So if you're asking the question: Would the MUP act as the detectives to see if there is a basis for a case, then that might be a different situation from the one that Mrs. Marinkovic understands by the use of the expression "investigation."

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'm guided, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Posing the question as Judge Bonomy has just indicated, were -- did the MUP act as the detectives for their own defendants, meaning if somebody was accusing a MUP member of murder or some egregious act, did the MUP itself serve as the detectives?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning the identification of a perpetrator of a crime, irrespective of who that is, the MUP is authorised pursuant to the public authorities -- public prosecutor's authority to gather data, collect evidence, and conduct interviews and to do anything that would assist in identifying the perpetrator. It doesn't matter whether it's an ordinary citizen, a policeman, male or female, an adult or minor. They act within that purview and they have to do their part in identifying the perpetrator, even if it's a policeman. There was a number of cases where I conducted the investigative proceedings and the policemen were -- policemen were perpetrators. There were such cases, I recollect them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Outside of the singular example that was shown to you on Friday with regards to the two policemen that were arrested and there was some public outcry, outside of that singular case when else were policemen indicated as being the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll object as far as this is not tied to the jurisdiction that the judge was in. There might be -- we heard there were courts in Prizren and elsewhere --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but the Court -- we --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would -- -

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- I certainly would read the question confined to her personal knowledge and experience --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That would be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And on that basis, it's perfectly proper.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Judge Marinkovic, you had indicated in your previous answer that: "There were a number of cases where I conducted the investigative proceedings and the policemen were the perpetrators ..." Outside of the singular example that was given on Friday, what other cases did you investigate where police were the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the air-strikes, there was a murder. I conducted both the on-site investigation and the investigating proceedings. The person in question was a reserve policeman, Slobodan Marusic, a.k.a. Boban. The murder took place in a bar. He came to the bar, which was packed, and one of the guests there was a military person who was on leave. That person had been injured and subsequently succumbed to the wounds on the way to the hospital. The person suspected of committing the crime was in detention and an indictment was issued and I believe the case was concluded and a judgement rendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I just wanted one clarification from you, Judge. You told us that a person could be detained even by MUP or other forces if they see him on the side or if they find him out to be a perpetrator. Now, I just wanted to know the duration of time when he could be detained before his production before a judge for formal arrest or indictment. What is the legal position on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the war and before the introduction of a state of war according to the Law on Criminal Procedure, when a member of the MUP killed a certain person, such a person could be detained until an indictment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You misspoke, you said when the MUP kills someone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. When the MUP takes someone into custody. I guess I misspoke. Thank you. Members of the MUP could keep that person in detention for 72 hours, three days, within which time they had to be handed over to an investigative judge with a criminal report submitted or to have the person handed over to the public prosecutor. During the times of war, there was a decree that was put in place regulating certain provisions of the Law on Criminal Procedure. The dead-line was extended. Organs of the MUP could have that person detained up to 30 days before turning that person over to an investigative judge, and it should be accompanied by a criminal report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: So when he was produced before an investigating judge like your good self, then you'd further hand over his custody to someone or send him to jail or what would you do? Will it be through a written order or will you produce him before a judicial court? How would you act then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When a person is detained and handed over to an investigative judge, after conducting an interview on all of the circumstances pursuant to an investigative request, I decide whether the public prosecutor's request was founded and then I decide on further detention. In this case I extended that detention. After that with that decision, the person is kept in detention during the entire duration of investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When we last spoke you'd indicated that you investigated the murder committed by Slobodan Marusic and also on Friday you spoke of Nikolic and Djeletovic. Are there any others that you are aware of where a MUP member is accused of murder or some other egregious act?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other cases. Now that you're asking me, I remember a case against a policeman by the name of Dragan Mitic or Matic. It concerned a murder of a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it was in late 1997 or so; however, I do remember the case and the person involved was a policeman. There was another case concerning a policeman, was it Milenkovic. In any case, a civilian had been killed; however, both cases were prior to 1998. I don't know the exact dates. There were such cases and the perpetrators were always kept in detention, indictments were issued, and judgements subsequently rendered, although I don't know exactly what sentences they received.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any murders taking place in 1998 or 1999 by policemen, outside of the ones that we've already discussed?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning my jurisdiction, that is the district court of Pristina, concerning the two cases involving murders -- well, apart from those two I had no other cases. I had cases involving other crimes. I cannot recall any other cases involving murder.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Let's expand the question to include cases against life and limb. Are you aware of any sort of, again, aggravated robberies, some sort of beatings, assaults, anything of that account?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, there was a case involving a robbery.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When did that occur?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was at the beginning of the war. The person was prosecuted, a report was submitted to the district prosecutor; however, that case remained in Pristina. It was not concluded due to many circumstances I have already described. This was not a case that would involve custody; therefore, the prosecutor could only submit a request through the regular channels and then conduct investigation accordingly. There were other cases, for example, involving property crimes; however, that falls under the competence of the municipal court. Therefore, they had many more reports submitted and those cases did not envisage detention.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: We have had evidence of looting throughout the wartime by both members of the VJ as well as the MUP. If you're dealing with members of the MUP participating in looting, would that be considered a property crime, thereby going to the municipal court?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when you say "looting," it is rather general. The crime of robbery and aggravated robbery, those are property crimes as well as theft, that falls under the competence of the municipal court. That involves taking away someone's property. I don't know whether you would strictly define it as robbery.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you please define for us what aggravated robbery would include that would be sent to a municipal court?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, "pljacka" is not part of the criminal law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, there is a translation issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe the witness is talking about the aggravated theft and not the aggravated -- and it is -- it has been translated over and over as aggravated robbery or robbery or aggravated robbery. She's talking about the theft, the simple theft, and the aggravated theft. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ma'am, what I'm focusing on is in many jurisdictions when the moniker "aggravated" is added to a crime it implies some sort of violence. Is that accurate with regards to the Serbian Criminal Code?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is theft and aggravated theft. The crime of theft is committed when someone takes another's property. And aggravated theft is robbing a house, taking property by committing burglary by entering the premises. Aggravated theft is more serious and it should involve robbery or breaking in, taking something away in that particular -- such particular means.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I think the best thing is to give her an illustration. Supposing on a highway a car is stopped and people are injured and their belongings removed, what would you call this as, an aggravated theft, a robbery, dacoity, what would you call it and what would be the punishment? I think that's the problem because theft is a different thing. What will happen on the roadside, highway, or going out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The example you cite contains several elements of robbery. It involves forced coercion and illegal taking away of property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I think that is what Ms. Carter is trying to say. She's not talking of theft, she is talking of the robbery of the kind which you now contemplate. Am I right, Ms. Carter?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What we're trying to determine is which type of crimes go to which courts. Now, you have indicated that property crimes go to the municipal court. Included within property crimes you had indicated that there's some sort of aggravated theft. At any time is there a theft crime that includes violence towards the victim that also goes to the municipal court?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to be specific. Concerning theft and aggravated theft, that fell under the purview of the municipal court given the sentence envisaged by law for such crimes. The municipal court is competent to hear cases which can be issued sentences of up to ten years --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Ten and over.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the crimes of robbery, including coercion and force, under the -- at the time it fell under the competence of the district court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. First of all, the witness is talking a bit fast, so I would ask her that she talks slowly because what we are getting in transcript is not what she is saying and it's very, very confusing. Actually, the Law on Criminal Procedure which is the evidence in this case is really very strict about it and there is an explanation on that, but just for the purposes of the record and now the municipal court -- the county court is in charge of all cases which are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've now introduced an expression --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- we haven't heard. Let's confine ourselves to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the district court. The district court tries the cases where the sentence can be -- that can be given is ten years or more. Municipal court tries the cases which had the sentences lower than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. That may be the theory and I understand that and I hope it's in a document somewhere and we don't really need this sort of examination for that, but one of the things that's been recorded in English as said by the judge so far is that cases went to the municipal court where custody was not envisaged at all, and that for theft -- property crimes in general, in fact, she said according to the English translation that custody was not envisaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I know that the theory is different, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is not what the witness said, that's why I'm saying the -- it is very confusing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, we do, do we not, have these rules as exhibits here? And what you really should be exploring are specific examples that the witness has some knowledge of that she can tell us how it operated in practice. Is that not the position?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the reason the questioning is being asked is because we have had any number of documents that have been admitted from the Defence in regards to investigations and proper criminal courts being run. Only until this witness has indicated that there are two separate courts. Most of the crimes that we're seeing are coming down to property crimes, theft, looting, that type of thing, and that's being shown that that's somehow a functioning judiciary. I'm trying to explore that bit, is there a difference between the municipal and the district and how each of them were functioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But we have documents that tell us that, don't we?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Not exactly, Your Honour. It -- there has never been an indication that there was a separate judicial system that somehow between a -- because they're always put in summaries, that somehow -- that the property crimes and the crimes against life or limb are all coming in to some of these massive exhibits. In doing so it indicates that it's all the same functioning judiciary. It appears that they're two separate judiciaries, and that's what I'm attempting to explore at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But don't we have documents about Serbian criminal procedure that tell us that there are municipal courts and district courts and that they have different sentencing powers.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: It does indicate that there are different sentencing powers; however, there appears to be a difference because again aggravated theft and robbery, depending on how you're reading it, seem to be very similar, and that's why I'm trying to explore with the witness, what is envisaged under municipal law, what is envisaged under the district court law, and I'll also follow up with the custody not envisaged inquiry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you're going to have to do it with simple questions that are very clear otherwise there is going to be confusion, because in interpretation the distinctions that we clearly understand between robbery and theft are not necessarily ones that are familiar to the interpreters. So you will have to be very specific with your questions. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to be of assistance a little. What municipal courts deal with in Serbia is none of your concern, take my word for it, those are petty thefts, pocket stealing, et cetera, somebody gets drunk --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, I don't think first of all -- I'm very sorry to cut you off. I don't think this is an appropriate stage for you to make these submissions. If we feel that the questions are not going to be helpful to us in the end, then we will intervene, but one of the Prosecution's -- one of the elements of the Prosecution's case is that the system didn't work as it ought to work. And for you to tell us and assert the situation is a matter for later based on the evidence, and you're not in a position to give us evidence. I know you're an expert in the field, but you're on nobody's 65 ter list, you're not being led as a witness. If we feel the need, and there may be a need, to have more assistance from counsel because of their experience, we will come to you. But so as not to prejudice the cross-examination, let's leave that till later. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ma'am, I'm going to attempt to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: To try to get some clarity, I'm going to ask you a series of hypothetical questions, where I would just like you to answer for me whether that case would go to a municipal court or a district court. The first example, if a person were to go to somebody else's yard and take some of their property, first off what would that crime be called and which court would handle it?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say "somebody else's property," we have to know what exactly was taken because "property" is a broad term and it can cover movable, immovable objects, we have to know what it is because it's one of the essential elements in qualifying a crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. What if the person goes and takes another person's car, what is that crime called and which court would deal with it?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, if we're talking about motor vehicles it can be theft but it can also be misappropriation, but in any case it's within the purview of the municipal court. Only if the car was locked and then the perpetrator used an object to forcibly open the door and start the vehicle using some inappropriate means, that would be aggravated theft because it involved breaking and entering, that makes it aggravated theft, but again the municipal court would be in charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So taking that into the houses. So if I were to break into a house, break open a lock, go into a house, and steal somebody's TV, is that again aggravated theft?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And that would still maintain in the municipal court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Same scenario with a couple of additional bits. I go -- I break into a house, I go inside, this time there are people in it. I forcibly remove from those people jewellery. What is that crime and which court does it go to?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when you say "forcibly," we have to identify how, whether by use of violence, by threat, or coercion. But if this violence is proven in any form, then it would have the elements of the criminal act of robbery and then the district court would be in charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So that's the change-over, in the event that there is violence towards a person, that rises it to the level of robbery which sends it to the district court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll now move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there was violence or if by using violence a serious or less-serious injury was inflicted, there are three or four paragraphs envisaging various forms of qualification. Only -- it's only a difference in sentencing.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And just to confirm, now you had said before that if it went to the municipal court that custody was not envisaged. So, so long as there's not violence towards the victim, custody would not be envisaged at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. The grounds for remand in custody are completely different. Custody is a measure to ensure the presence of the accused. It has nothing to do with the qualification of the criminal acts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think that's the question, although I understand why you're answering it that way. There was a suggestion of a different English explanation from the language used earlier in one of your answers. If a person is guilty of aggravated theft, can that person be sentenced to a period of imprisonment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They can. If there are legal grounds to define remand in custody, such as danger that he might escape, that he might not be detectable, that he might influence witnesses or accomplices --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please stop. I can't understand this difficulty. I'm not asking about being remanded in custody. I was very specific in using the expression "sentenced" to a period of imprisonment. If a person is guilty, that word I also used, of aggravated theft, can that person be sentenced to a period of imprisonment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is the maximum if they're in the municipal court ten years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And if they go to the district court for robbery, as you've just told us would be appropriate, can they be sentenced to less than ten years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I now want to move on to the concept of direct filing is the term I would tend to use. You indicated yesterday that apart from the organs of the Ministry of the Interior who filed criminal reports for crimes that must be prosecuted ex officio, criminal reports may also be filed by other institutions of the state and by citizens, natural persons. Every citizen has the right to file a criminal report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Would that report be sent to you or to the MUP? Is that a yes?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, depending on whether the citizen knows to whom to file the report, he may file it directly to the MUP and he may file it also to the public prosecutor. And then the public prosecutor may redirect the criminal report to the MUP so that the MUP may check the allegations. Normally a criminal report is not filed with the investigative judge, but if the citizen doesn't know these things and files it nevertheless to the investigative judge, the investigative judge would then forward it either to the public prosecutor or to the SUP depending on the criminal act involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If the person was not sophisticated enough to know the proper procedure yet you became aware that a crime had been committed, would you have a duty to file some sort of report?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My duty as investigative judge would not be to file the criminal report, but to send that submission or letter to the public prosecutor because he is competent to judge whether there are any grounds to believe that a criminal act had been perpetrated and who the perpetrator is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I have just a little clarification to request for. Supposing nobody complains but a crime has taken place, who's going to report in such circumstances? Will the police do it or will it be -- how will the process of law put into operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's the duty of the police as soon as they find out that a crime has been committed to file a criminal report, and it's filed with the public prosecutor depending -- regardless of whether it's an identified or unidentified perpetrator. If it's a criminal act that is prosecuted ex officio, it is the duty of the MUP to file a criminal report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would like to bring up in e-court P3095?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ma'am, were you aware that as of 10 April 1986 the court president, Djordje Aleksic, of the district court in Pristina had issued this mandate that indicated that preference was to be given to cases involving Serbian and Montenegrin victims? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time the president of the court was Djordje Aksic, not Aleksic. It must be a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Were you aware of this provision when you became a judge there in 1984?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, it was a long time ago, but I do remember we had such instructions from the president of the court.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Were you aware of this provision ever being revoked in the Pristina district court?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. Maybe it was for that year because every year we received new instructions. And this one, let me tell you, had to do with the following. In that period a large number of Serbs and Montenegrins had started to leave Kosovo and Metohija and to move out from Kosmet because of all sorts of pressure they were under, and that's why we had been given suggestions on how to work with these cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You had indicated on Friday that --

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I read here at the bottom it says exactly until what time we had to draft that report. Every judge had to make a separate report by 18th April 1986 covering all the cases they were working on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So you're saying that this type of provision in the Pristina district court occurred only in 1986 and it was not carried through thereafter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember. Maybe we had the same instruction the following year. I really couldn't say now. It was a long time ago. I didn't especially pay attention to a document like this, it didn't stick in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I ask because you had indicated during your direct examination that it seemed to be quite a congenial area where Serbs and Albanians and other ethnicities were all getting along, but it appears that there's going to be some sort of preferential treatment with regards to some victims. I'm trying to decide when that preferential treatment cut off?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, I really couldn't say. I wouldn't agree that it was preferential because it was a kind of updating of these cases. As for my movement and my contacts with people of other ethnicities, nothing had changed and there were no problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Why would there be a provision within the district court of Pristina to only update the cases of Serbs and Montenegrins as opposed to, say, the Kosovar Albanians?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, at that time it was the human rights of the Serbs and other non-Albanians in Kosovo and Metohija that were in much greater danger than those of Albanians. I suppose that's one of the reasons. The wish was to stop the moving out, and that's why this instruction was given to update cases where the injured parties were Serbs and Montenegrins.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: This is around the same time that the speech was given at Kosovo Polje where Milosevic indicated, You will not be beaten; and those type of marches. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you honestly, I don't remember that. If you have a document saying that it was so, I'll take your word for it. I was never involved in politics and I cannot tell you anything with any precision.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: However, your household was involved in politics, were they not? In fact, your husband was taking part in those revolutions; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have a document proving that, it must be so.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In fact you testified to that in the Milosevic case, did you not, that your husband was a part of those demonstrations, that The Serbs would get the status that they deserved in Kosovo and Metohija, those are your words at transcript page 37931, lines 17 through 19.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's the way I said it there, it must be correct. I am not retracting on my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to move on to the providence of 6D586. This is an exhibit that has been entered as a 92 ter statement of yours where it's serving as a summary of a number of cases. You had indicated in the Milosevic case that the cases that make up that summary were those that you managed to save when you left in Kosovo and these were something that remain in your possession. Are these documents that make up the background of 5D -- excuse me, 6D586, are they the original court documents?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I give an explanation beforehand, I did not say and it's not true that I had succeeded in taking the case files with me and that it had been submitted. Those are just parts of the indictments and parts of the judgements, because all the case files, those of my cases and my colleagues, remained in Pristina. And after the signing of the Kumanovo Agreement the representatives of the ICTY - that's how they introduced themselves - came together with some Albanians and the KFOR and gathered all the case files before they had been listed. And I don't know whether those case files had been returned, where they had been taken from, or they are still kept here at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ma'am, I would hold out to you that in the Milosevic case at transcript page 37727, which has actually been uploaded into e-court at P3115, page 15, you indicated that this is what you managed to save when you went from Kosovo, you go on at page 16 in the e-court and say that this is something that remains in her possession -- or your possession, these are things that were actually stated by Milosevic with regards to the providence of these documents. So and I'm trying to determine, were these documents the court files?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And were these the original court files that you kept in your possession or were they copies?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The originals were in my possession and these are photocopies.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So you kept in your own personal archive the originals of the cases that are addressed in 6D586?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Why wouldn't you leave official court files with the court as opposed to taking them with you?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, official court files stayed with the court. This is just a single copy because when an indictment or a judgement is typed up several copies are made, and then my colleagues distributed one of those copies to me because I had been in charge of the investigation. I was supposed to follow those cases through all the way to the final result, and this is something that is perfectly legitimate.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I've got a quick question on the court documents. In official court documents, what is the name used for Albanians? Can you both state it and spell it.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not sure I understand your question. Albanians, what other name could there possibly be?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Well, we've heard in this courtroom that there's a term called Siptar and that there are other terms such as Albanac. I want to know in official court documents what word is used to designate Albanian ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Albanian, and they actually had a court interpreter for Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you please spell for me which word was used when designating Albanian in official court documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I will have to object at this time because I think my learned colleague should ask in -- in which language as well because we know that the Albanian and Serbian are both used in Kosovo as official languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Actually, I will address more specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In 6D588, which is listed from 1993, I would hold out to you that the name that is used in the original court document for Albanians is Albanac, A-l-b-a-n-a-c, and not Siptar. Are you aware of that? You can look to the very first page of it. All of these defendants are of Albanian ethnicity and each are listed as Albanac, the first one beginning at the third line.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you really need to do as Mr. Zecevic suggested so that the transcript is clear. This is which language?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What language were the official court files stated in?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both languages were used as official languages, Serbian and Albanian. So both languages were used for documents and whatever part is required an Albanian translation, their requests were complied.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: But the language --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question -- sorry, on you go.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What language is 6D588 in?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This indictment was written in Serbian, but there was also an Albanian copy and it was served on all of the parties involved in their own mother tongue.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: However, in the Serbian copy beginning at least in 1993 when designating a person of Albanian ethnicity, the word "Albanac" is used in the Serbian; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What language is on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Serbian, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Pardon me --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The indictment is in Serbian, and on the right-hand side we see an English translation I assume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And this Serbian indictment is written in Latin script. Is that because the persons involved are Albanian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It depended on the typewriter used, there were Cyrillic ones and Latin script ones, and at the time we were using Latin script typewriters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ma'am, I would now direct your attention to 6D589. This is a court document dated 1995, and I would hold out to you that again -- well, first of all, can you identify the language used in 6D589?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will that be shown on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: It will be shown on the screen, but it's also in the notebooks that you've received.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 589, right?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes. Can you please tell me what language is 6D589 written in?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. And again, in the Serbian the word for Albanian is being used "Albanac," A-l-b-a-n-a-c, in official court documents in 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would now direct you to a 1997 indictment, and that will be 6D587. Can you please identify the language for me.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And again, the word that's being used is not "Siptar," but rather "Albanac"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we do not have another document provided after 1997, so I'm just going to have to ask you. In the Serbian court documents of the Pristina district court, was it ever changed where "Albanac" was not used but rather "Siptar"?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Would you ever expect to find the word "Siptar" in any sort of legal document?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: There has been testimony in this case that "Siptar" is a word like any other with no foul intent to it. What I want to know is: Would you expect to ever see the word "Siptar" in any sort of indictment, order, or any sort of legal document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'll -- rather than persuading the witness, I'll let her answer, but then I do have a comment after the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ma'am, can you tell me, would you expect to ever see the word "Siptar" in any sort of indictment, appellate judgement, court order, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say is this, I spent a long time in Pristina from 1976 onwards. People who were natives of the area --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, please think of the question and please answer the question. It's related to your experience of indictments and other court documents, not about the practice of people in general in their relationships in Pristina. That can be explored if others wish to explore it further in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ma'am, I would reiterate my question. In court documents, be it an indictment, appellate judgement, or any sort of official court order, would you expect to see the word "Siptar" used?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as my work was concerned, the term "Albanian" was always used because that's what those people declared themselves to be. If there was a trial one would ask them, What's your ethnicity, and they would say Siptar. They didn't mind. It wasn't a derogatory term or anything [as interpreted], this was a term that they had always used themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ma'am, you indicated: "As far as my work was concerned, the term 'Albanian' was always used ..." now, when you used the word "Albanian," were you using this word spelled A-l-b-a-n-a-c?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to move on to a specific case that you handled, specifically 6D589 --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Before counsel moves on, we do have a transcript error at page 40, lines 15 through 17, at the end of the witness's answer she said they didn't mind, it wasn't a derogatory term or anything, this was a term they had always used themselves previously is I think the most concise addition to that. And for the record, since counsel's question was: If there was ever any official court document calling someone Siptar, the United Nations indictment in this case officially translated by CLSS has Siptar and Siptari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just identify the paragraph, Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, on you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Page 40, paragraphs -- 14 through 18 is the entire answer, but I think the part that was omitted is at the end of 18, where the witness said that they had used that themselves previously or in the past --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I follow that. That's redundant. I mean, you can only use things in the past -- if you use the word "had," it must always be in the past. But I'm more interested on the page in the indictment on which in reference can be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The entire Albanian version, Your Honour, based on recollection. If the Court requires, I could check that and present a written memorandum or submission just to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the way to deal with that is to ask questions of the witness. The indictment's a perfectly legitimate document to be used --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- in examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is and that's why I withdrew the objection as soon as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But my reason for asking you is that repeatedly through the English version the expression is simply Kosovo Albanians, and I thought you were referring to the English official indictment when you said the word "Siptar" was used, but I take it your comment is confined to the Albanian translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not the Serb?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't think I've ever actually looked at the Serb version of the indictment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You may have more questions in re-examination than you thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It seems like it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would this be a suitable opportunity for us to take our break, Ms. Carter?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, we have a break now for half an hour. Could you please leave the court with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall resume at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Ivetic, you caught me when I wasn't thinking, but thinking about it immediately after leaving the court is Siptar not the obvious word to use in an Albanian version of the indictment because that is the word for Albanian? And I think it says Siptari Kosoves.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct, that's been our point to since day one that Siptar is not a derogatory term as CLSS has in one fell swoop made it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but we dealt with that, as you know, earlier and the whole point of that remark is the use of the word Siptar in a Serb-language document, which is a completely different thing from the use of the word Siptar in an Albanian-language document. So I was slightly misled -- I misled myself, but I think I'm now clear on the issue so far as it relates to the indictments. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Judge Marinkovic, I would direct your attention to 6D589 in your binder of documents. You had discussed that case pretty thoroughly in as two -- sorry, transcript 23516, starting at line 14, last Monday. This case is the -- basically the illegal MUP case from the KLA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry -- no, please continue. I'll interrupt you in a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document is in reference to the illegal MUP. There are no members of the KLA MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you just give us a moment, please, Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm very sorry about that, Ms. Carter. There was a matter troubling us which I think we've now resolved. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No apologies needed, Your Honour. That's why you wear the red robe. You get to do whatever you want in your courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Judge Marinkovic, do you believe that this illegal MUP case was professionally handled by all parties involved?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean 590, the judgement?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: 589 is the indictment, I believe, and 590 is the judgement, yes. Do you believe that case was professionally handled by all parties involved?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Were you aware that out of the 70 indictees that make up 6D589, ten of them were beaten while incarcerated during the investigation?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. If you have a document to show me to that effect, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Absolutely. And just to remind you, you actually were discussing these beatings in the Milosevic case beginning at page 37937 which is here in e-court at P3115, beginning at page 225, but specifically I would like to bring to your attention the medical reports beginning with the first defendant, defendant number one, at P3101 is the medical certificate about what occurred to Avdija Mehmedovic. You actually signed the order in order to have this man observed, and it was indicated that he had damage to his right palm, to his left palm, as well as the central and frontal part of his lower legs, that in fact those were excoriated and exposed skin is dry and the scab had to be removed and that this was caused by a heavy blow from a blunt heavy mechanical implement. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the medical finding, but beating is a generic term. That is the first thing I have to say. It can cover a multitude of situations. I would not agree that this is a case of beating. I do see this finding, the medical finding, with the doctor saying that only a slight injury was sustained.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ma'am, what would you call an injury being afflicted [sic] by a heavy blow from a blunt heavy mechanical implement, what would you call that if not beating?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not within the jurisdiction and authority of the judge to make determinations like that. She is not a doctor and I believe under the criminal procedure system in the FRY that the prosecution would handle cases of that nature. So I think that this question is outside the bound width of what the witness can be competent on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. The witness herself, though, has raised the point by saying that beating is a generic term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think we are going to be usefully assisted Ms. Carter by an exchange of views about beating unless it has a technical definition which in some legal systems it may have, but the witness has said it's generic in her experience which suggests there isn't a technical definition. It's a matter of the interpretation of the context, is it not, which is at the end of the day a matter for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And along those lines, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ma'am, it is a generic term, it's generic because this type of injury, specifically a heavy blow from a blunt heavy mechanical implement, happened not only one time but against ten separate defendants in this case, did it not?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, I can't remember this specifically.
