If you have a document such as this one, I'm sure then that this was the case; however, as to how these injuries were inflicted by what instrument and the types of injuries themselves, I'm no expert in those matters and that's why I sent an order to the forensic institute to establish this, what sort of injury occurred, did such injuries exist. You've shown me one such finding, and it would have been down to the prosecutor had the existence of such injuries ever been ascertained, they would have known what to do about it. It's not job to study the manner in which these injuries came about, what those injuries were, or who they were inflicted by if indeed this was the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: To complete the first line I would hold out to you the defendant number 7 Bljerim Oloni his medical report is at P3100; defendant 13, Ramadan Ferizi his medical report is at P3102, all of these taking place on the 14th of December. Moving on to the 15th of December we have the medical reports of defendant 21 -- excuse me out of 6D589 Bejtulah Alidema at P3104; a defendant 38, Tahir Caka at P3103; and defendant number 4, Seremet Ahmeti at P3099. A full week later you have another series of defendants of this case that all contain similar language to being -- having a heavy blow by a heavy mechanical object and that's defendant 10 Murat Sahiti at P3105; defendant 27 Isak Aliu at P3096; defendant 35, Kemalj Aliu at P3098; and defendant 39, Sali Bruti at P3097. Given that you had ten members of the same case all receiving injuries that are consistent with a heavy blow from a blunt object, are you aware of any sort of prosecution or investigation into the injuries inflicted upon these defendants?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, you're trying to say that there's a pattern?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: That's if you tell it like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ma'am, there is a pattern of beating -- sorry, a pattern of injuries being inflicted by a blunt force by a mechanical object. With this pattern was this ever investigated or anybody ever identified for prosecution?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue at hand is not a matter of pattern, it is rather the instrument and manner of -- used to inflict injuries. If you look at the dates in the indictment and the dates of detention, it means that at that moment I had interviewed them as an investigative judge. There's a time span of ten and more days between that and the findings; therefore, the time of injuries is important, the place, the manner, the gravity of injuries, and everything else. It is all pertinent. You mentioned all of the dates which are in mid-December 1994 concerning the findings shown. It is most likely that the defendant himself or that his attorney complained concerning his medical status and in keeping with the law. I ordered the institute to conduct an examination of those persons in order to ascertain what the issue at hand is --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ma'am, let me stop you there. Again I'm going to reiterate my question. Was anyone investigated or anybody identified for prosecution based on these injuries received on the ten defendants?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that the witness be allowed to continue her answer. Again, she's explaining what's within her competence I believe, and as I had mentioned before there is a system in place in the SFRY that perhaps is unfamiliar just to -- to other legal jurisprudences, but it's -- it's akin to asking a question of a police officer what the fire department does. I mean, the witness is answering within her competence what she did and she's entitled to give that answer and to provide what she did. And the fact that the prosecution's office is not happy with the answer they're getting is of no relevance.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the sidebar comments made by Defence counsel and I would also argue that this witness is not answering the question asked. I specifically asked: Were these member -- was anybody prosecuted for these injuries? And given that the witness quite distinctly indicated over Friday that she was involved in this case and in fact includes within her documents all documents up to and including the final judgement of these defendants, she certainly would be in a position to be able to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, she has given you the answer that she thinks that she instructed the investigation of -- by the pathologists involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, she indicated that she did -- because as you can see within those documents that I indicated, the medical investigations, that she did sign off requesting that that be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What I'm trying to determine --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: -- is once this was received what if anything happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you interrupted her answer, which is what Mr. Ivetic is saying, because she said that this was done in order to ascertain what the issue at hand is. Now could you tell us what emerged once you got these reports. What did you do about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to continue and you are correct, I was interrupted by the Prosecutor. When I received the reports, I forwarded a copy to the attorney representing the defendant and the set of documents pertaining to these people was forwarded to the relevant public prosecutor. This is where my competence ends. The public prosecutor, based on the documents received, assesses whether any further investigation will be done. If they believe there are elements of crime and that there is a need to identify perpetrators, then it is within their purview to undertake measures to follow that up, to see whether it indeed happened. As to whether there were any proceedings instituted, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In regards to this case, you also indicated in Friday's testimony that you issued an order disallowing the Defence attorneys from reviewing the file and participating in certain investigative procedures, did you not?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And I would hold out to you that that document was issued five days after you received the final reports about the beatings -- I'm sorry, about the injuries sustained within this case. Isn't that correct? You issued that order on the 27th of December, 1997, and these injuries were all documented by the 22nd of December. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the exact dates. Perhaps you can show me the document you're referring to so that I can compare the dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I call up P3106.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I show you the beginning indicating the top right-hand corner indicating the date of December 27th, 1994, and I would move you to page 3 of that document, page 2 in the B/C/S, where it indicates your rulings.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that this is the document is of the 26th of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Judge Marinkovic, I would hold out to you the indication that you gave to this court is after receiving the documents that these individuals had sustained injuries you sent it on for processing, sent it on to the Defence attorneys and they -- whatever happened from there was not in your province. But I would indicate to you that you interjected yourself into that because five days after you issued an order disallowing the defence attorneys from even reviewing the file, did you not?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you tell me what your question is specifically, what is it that you want to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just for the record, Your Honour, I think this is part of clearly in the direct examination we're talking about the investigative pre-indictment stage at which point I don't know whether it's a file or a case at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's leave the parties, Mr. Ivetic, the counsel and the witness to deal with this between themselves. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ma'am, I would direct you to page 3 in the English and page 2 in the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but the order speaks for itself. What's your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: My question is, Your Honour, that --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Well, ma'am --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: She did issue the order; there's no dispute about that. So what's the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ma'am, if you indicated that you sent in for processing the investigation on these ten injuries, yet you in turn close the file to the defence attorneys. Do you believe that that could have been properly investigated or properly reviewed by their counsel?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I still do not comprehend. The medical documentation doesn't have anything to do with the case itself and concerning the perpetrator or the crime committed or it has no relation to any material evidence existing. This medical documentation could be an indication for another case file to be opened precisely because of the contents of those documents. Therefore, this decision on my part had nothing to do with the documentation mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ma'am, you indicated that the procedure once you received these medical reports was that you delivered that material to the defence attorneys and it went on for any sort of investigation as needed. Are you telling me that closing the file to the very same defence attorneys was an appropriate action?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, you would need to establish, first of all, that there's some link between the two. The file is the file in relation to the investigation of the allegations. The medical position was submitted to both defence attorneys and the prosecutor for them to take whatever action they considered appropriate, which the witness has told you would, if necessary, have involved raising or opening a new file on a new case alleging beating. What's the link? What's that got to do with the file in the investigative process?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Specifically, Your Honour, that once the file is closed and once these defence attorneys are prohibited from full participation in the investigation, if anything were to continue, any more beatings, any more issues -- the defence attorneys weren't even in the position to be able to communicate with their clients, and that is something that this witness specifically did by issuing the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, does the order prevent them from communicating with their clients?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: It indicates from attending certain investigative activities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that's nothing to do with the medical injuries they had sustained by the allegation of beating.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it seems a bit odd that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's a matter for submissions later, but I -- please bear in mind I at the moment don't see the link. If you can establish a link, then perhaps we can make some progress. No, please, just listen to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Carter, do you -- are you trying to think of any further torture while they were in custody and are you thinking of any torture?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would argue that anything described in the way that these ten reports did out of the single case would rise to the level of torture, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: No, you mean further to these injuries, another torture while in custody?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: That is conceivable, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: No, the question would be did they have the opportunity of getting themselves medically examined, because if they will get themselves medically examined and they are injured further then that would be a complaint because that's the way.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I will back up then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ma'am, you indicated that an order was issued to stop the Defence counsel from involving themselves in certain aspects of the investigation. Can you please be more specific. What were the defence counsel disallowed from doing starting on 27 December 1994?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not issue an order. It was a decision on my part, in keeping with my competences under the Law on the Criminal Procedure, which is Article 73, Article 2, and Article 168, paragraph 5, as stated in the decision. I'm authorised to do that, and at the given moment on the proposal of the public prosecutor I assessed that it was in the interests of the state and its security as well as its defence to have this put into place, that there are justified reasons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not -- again, Judge Marinkovic, that's not the question. The question is: What were the certain investigative activities that the defence were not permitted to participate in? It's not clear from the order. It just uses the -- well, the English word used is "certain" investigative activities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the decision, perhaps we can go back a bit, we have the measures described specifically. Could we please have that on the monitor. I can only see the second page here. We didn't -- we don't see the pronouncement itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: For ease of the witness I can provide a hard copy of both pages so she can have each in front of her at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do we not have the English version of the order either then?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's P3106.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, but are we on the wrong page?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, the third page of the English indicated that the investigative judge has found grounds for the proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's the ruling we need to see here.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Page 2, it lists the requests to the prosecutors and then the finding that the investigative judge has found grounds for the proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that page doesn't give it in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour, it does. The very final thing it says: "Therefore, security reasons demand that the defendants at this stage of the proceedings be denied access to files" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I'm not reading that on the page I'm looking at, Ms. Carter. I'm trying to get the English page in front of me that deals with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: It's page 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's the page we had before and that doesn't specify what the activities are.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the very final sentence right above -- it says the above ruling, final paragraph it says: "Therefore, security reasons demand that the defendants at this stage of the proceeding be denied access to files and collected evidence and not be present during certain investigative activities" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Correct, I understand that. So what are certain investigative activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: That was my question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it was mine about ten minutes ago, and Mrs. Marinkovic tells us it's set out somewhere in the order. So can you direct us, Mrs. Marinkovic - it's not an order, I apologise - where in the decision will we see the specific investigative activities which the defence are not permitted to participate in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the decision itself, towards the bottom, I don't know if it says the same in English, but it says they are prevented from studying the files and inspecting physical evidence as well as attending certain investigative activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what are these investigative activities that they are prevented from attending? That's all we want to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For example, a witness interview, if there were any witness interviews in the case or if there were any investigative activities as such. We have in this case as evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that means they can't attend any investigative activities; is that what it means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that moment, apart from attending defendant interviews, other investigative activities were prohibited for defence counsel to attend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you've already told us that the defendant interviews were already done and finished?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What precisely had the defendants done at this stage of the proceeding that required this finding to be made, that they cannot participate in certain investigative activities?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the defendants were charged with the crime of associating for hostile activities and the crime of violating the constitutional order, since it goes directly against the constitutional basis of the state, following an application by the public prosecutor this decision was put in place since it was in the interest of the country, its security, and defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If that is the actual reason, why wasn't this order issued at the inception of the case? Why was there a delay?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. I don't see where you're going. I believe my previous answer was sufficiently clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Judge Marinkovic, your indictment was issued on 7 April 1995. It indicates throughout - and this is at 6D589 - it indicates that all of these men were brought into custody in late November of 1994, yet they serve in detention for over a month prior to you issuing this order. I want to find out what intervening action took place that made you issue this order.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, I cannot be very specific since at the given moment it was simply our assessment that the interests of security and defence of the state were at stake. As to what specific activities were undertaken, I don't know. Many years have passed. In terms of physical evidence pertaining to this case, a number of disks was retrieved and they had to be gone through in order to see what the contents were --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'm more specific --

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- whether there was anything illegal concerning --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'm more specific in my question. What occurred while these men were in detention that caused you to issue an order to disallow the defence attorneys access to certain investigative activities as well as access to the case file?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, in the investigative phase nothing necessarily needed to happen. However, the factual situation pointed at the importance of one such decision to be put in place, and it was temporary until an indictment was issued by the district public prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So you're indicating that the indictment was issued on several -- on 7 April 1995, so from the end of December through April 1995 these defendants were not allowed access to the court file or their defence attorneys were not allowed access to the court file or to be participating in the investigation?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see the whole indictment and I don't know when I concluded the whole investigation. Once that was done, I forwarded the entire file to the public prosecutor, and they require a certain amount of time to issue an indictment. Therefore, that time-period may overlap with the documents being with the public prosecutor. They were preparing themselves, deciding against who to issue indictments.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: During this investigative phase, when if ever did you take statements from these defendants?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the investigation, in this case after they were once heard or interviewed by the investigative judge there was no need for me to interview them again. This should only take place if there were any amendments or expanding of the scope of the investigation in order to include other persons, and this could be done by the public prosecutor in relation to that case. Therefore, I re-interviewed those persons again. Concerning this decision, I don't know whether the prosecutor heard the legal remedy. Anyone who wasn't happy with the decision I made in the investigative phase could appeal, and it was submitted to the counsel of the district court in Pristina. If people were dissatisfied with the decision, they could have forwarded a complaint to the district court in Pristina penal chamber. If I was mistaken in pronouncing this decision --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ma'am, I'm going to reiterate my question. During the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but I maybe I might be of some help here; 59, 14, it was submitted to the counsel of district court, it is a specific chamber that decides on the appeal in that stage of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you. The question you were asked, Mrs. Marinkovic, is when you took statements from or interviewed the defendants.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Statements from the accused were taken within the legal dead-line when they were remanded in custody and turned over to me as the investigative judge. What is written here is when they were in custody, but the dates differ from the date when the decision to remand them in custody was made.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Did you interview these individuals after you issued the order disallowing their defence counsel from participating in certain investigative activities?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, because that is not allowed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicated that these people came in, the investigative judge interviewed them, and then at page 59, line 60, you said: "Therefore, I re-interviewed these persons again. If they were only in custody for approximately one month prior to you issuing that order when did those interviews take place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Give me that line again.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Just hold up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: She said there was no need for me to interview them again.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: At 59, 11, Your Honour, it says: "Therefore, I re-interviewed those people again."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can see the circumstances in which that would be appropriate. If there was a change in the indictment, then that would become appropriate. The witness has said several times that the interviews were long over before any of this was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Mrs. --

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just explain one thing to the Chamber. If you look at this decision of mine, you will see at the top the KIO number and then number 161 with different letters. All these were expansions. The first one related to Avdija Mehmedovic. What follows are various extensions under which I continued to work. And when the investigation was complete, when I had heard all the accused, then the decision was made applying to all these persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Judge Marinkovic, when I'm asking you questions, if I'm asking you specifically about a single case if we can deal with what happened in that case as opposed to what generally happens. I think that's causing some of the difficulties that we're having. So you have indicated that at no time were these individuals interviewed without presence of their counsel, is that correct, in this case?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said because it can't happen that way. Now I can explain the right to defence, in which case -- in which case as the presence of the defence counsel is obligatory and in which cases it is up to the accused to decide whether he wants his defence counsel to be present or not. In this group everybody had at least one, but usually two or three defence counsel. Some did not -- want an appointed counsel, and in other cases the crime involved did not require a defence attorney to be present and that was recorded always in the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: With regard --

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they themselves waived the right to counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: With regard to the ten individuals that we have medical reports on, did you at any time interview these people outside of the presence of their defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to look at the minutes that I kept at that time. I cannot remember specifically for each person. Avdija Mehmedovic is the only one that stands out in my memory because the first time he was supposed to make a statement before me, he and his defence counsel required on that day an adjournment of 24 hours because the accused or the defence counsel were tired and short on sleep. So I granted them a delay of 24 hours, and the next day they came at the appointed time. Everybody had the right if they did not want to appear on the appointed day.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now, at page 61, beginning at line 18, it says you "can now explain the right to defence, in which case the presence of the defence counsel was obligatory and in which cases it is up to the accused to decide whether he wants his defence counsel to be present ..." Did the court have the authority to prohibit -- this is generally speaking. Did the court have the right to prohibit defence counsel if the defendant wanted it from attending interviews and other investigative activities, specifically the interviews?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You have indicated that there are certain times when defence counsel is obligatory and sometimes when defence counsel's presence can be waived at the request of the defendant himself. What I'm asking is: Does the court have the right to prohibit contact between defence counsel and their defendant?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It is the right of the defence counsel to be in communication with his client.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Does the court have the right at any time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Carter. Are you wanting to say that does the investigating judge, not the court in that sense, I think she's confused, has the right to prohibit a counsel from joining the investigative process. Are you saying that or differently?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I am saying in regards to the type of order that we have seen that was in place in the case that's listed at 6D589, was there any other type of similar order that could be issued that would prohibit defence counsel from being able to communicate with their client or be present when their client is being interviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: And by this you mean by the investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ma'am, does the court, and specifically, does the investigative judge, meaning you, do you have the right to have client contact supervised or impose yourself or the keepers of the defendant into the contact between the client and the defence attorney?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You must start that question again and please ask it in clear English.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You have indicated that the court cannot stop defence counsel from being able to communicate with their client. Based on that, can the court impose certain criteria in regards to that contact, such as supervision or monitored correspondence?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, is Ms. Carter asking about what the law permits or what the judge is empowered under the law permit. I'm confused by the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, they would both amount to the same thing I assume. What's misleading -- I thought you were asking questions about preventing communication between counsel and client; now you've moved to something else without getting that one answered. You're now on to present supervision.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, I am still speaking of the communication between client and counsel. We've learned that you can't stop that communication. I want to see can you limit that communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's not confined to an interview by an investigative judge, this is in general?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: This is in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, if you would just ask that simple question we might get the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Judge Marinkovic, can you limit the communication between an investigative -- I'm sorry, between a client and his defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot limit their communication. The defence counsel may communicate with his client whenever he's able to. The only limitation is the house rules of the detention facility. If there are many inmates and there is not enough time to ensure visits for everyone on a certain day, a list is made saying that defence counsel may visit their clients between 1000 and 1400 hours. It is again a matter of the house rules of the detention facility that when the defence counsel is talking to his client they do so in the presence of the guards who are -- who do not take part in the discussion, they just stand there for security reasons and monitor the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, is there a live issue somewhere in this case about counsel not being allowed to communicate with Albanian accused that we are spending a lot of time on this. There must be something hidden in there that so far hasn't emerged.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, again we're talking about the functioning of the judiciary, the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but our lives aren't long enough to explore the functioning in general of the Serb judiciary, and we really have to get to the issues that actually relate to the present case. And at the moment we're dealing with one that doesn't even fall into 1998 and 1999 at extraordinary length.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- in the pre-trial brief at paragraph 145 we were indicating that while the judiciary was functioning, there is a difference between the way Serbian defendants are being treated and the way Albanian defendants are being treated. That is what I'm trying to explore. I'm also trying to explore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we have Prosecution evidence to that effect, do we?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is already evidence from the Prosecution in the case to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the first judge that is dealing with the MUP side. We do have VJ evidence in regards to the judiciary, but this is going to be the first instance that we're going to be able to explore extensively with the Court and I would say that -- and I do plan on showing a number of documents beginning with the one that we've just seen and through the time that's directly implicated by the witness that many of these provisions that she says are sacrosanct were actually violated in the Pristina district court, and I would offer P3109, I'd like that to be brought up and we can address a 30 October 1996 order that will keep us closer into time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the problem I have with the manner in which this is being presented by Ms. Carter now, as I recall they did not even lead any positive evidence in the OTP case issued from this issue, and to me it sounds like they're trying to now re-open the case that perhaps show one side or perhaps show an incomplete picture. The way it's phrased here, it might just be my reading of it but it just doesn't sound very encouraging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As you know, Mr. Ivetic, one of the hazards of leading Defence evidence is that the Prosecution case can get better. Indeed it is often the result of the presentation of a Defence case, there's no rule against that in this system. So please continue, Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would show you P3109, focusing on page 1 in the B/C/S as well as the English. In the middle where it's discussing the decision it indicates there's a lawyer by the name of Kelmendi. Was this the same attorney that you were speaking of earlier today that you found to be a very professional and appropriate attorney?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see here in the disposition.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now, in many of these cases there are joint accused, such as what we're doing here in court today, is that correct, in many of the cases that you handled?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In this it indicates that attorneys, including the very professional one that you had commented on, are refused to attend execution of some investigative measures, such as interrogation of the accused, except for their own accused, the confrontation of witnesses and hearing of witnesses, and to examine documents and records, except for records on interview with their defendants, as well as to examine items that might be of evidence. When you were dealing with these multiple accused cases, did you use evidence brought by one accused against the others?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, again this is an investigative judge, it's not a -- she's not a trial judge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, she has been in trials, Mr. Ivetic. Mrs. Marinkovic gave evidence earlier that when she wasn't involved in investigations she was part of a trial chamber, so she can deal with the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this decision that I see on the screen has to do with a case where I did the investigation, and I made a decision like in the previous case. It's the same decision, same legal grounds. I don't know what to comment on. The only thing that I can say about this case is that a large number of the accused were on the run. So I had not had the chance to question them, and therefore the presence of the defence counsel was a moot issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, the matter is a much more specific one again. In your procedure in general, can the things said by one accused person be used in the file of a case against another accused person if they are jointly accused. We've got six accused here, for example. Now, it's -- the case is being conducted as one trial, and the question that Ms. Carter's asking you is: If you took statements from one accused in an interview and he said things against one of the other accused, could you use that against the other accused as part of the case dossier against him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This may be done when an indictment is issued, and at the trial the judge compares the statements of respective accused and he may use whatever evidence is available to decide whether somebody was a perpetrator or an accomplice, in light of course of all the other evidence in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Judge Marinkovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, but this really needs some explanation to be done in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Because our law --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I don't want you to explain because Mrs. Marinkovic's own knowledge of matters may become an issue in relation to her reliability as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is a matter for re-examination not for submissions --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I understand very well, but I just thought that Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- not be misled with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed. I understand your concern, and at the end of the evidence if you think that there is something in there that could well mislead us and you as a responsible court officer feel it ought to be drawn to our attention, that would be the time to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Judge Marinkovic, were you aware that in 1997 the Pristina district court, and even you specifically, were brought to the attention of the UN Commission on Human Rights in regards to a report of the Special Rapporteur of the situation of human rights in the territory of the former Yugoslavia? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody ever told me at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would bring up P3090. Unfortunately at this point this is only in the English. Any bits of it that have to be translated will be done so.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Judge Marinkovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And specifically referring to page 2, paragraph 15 of this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Judge Marinkovic, the UN report indicates that within the Pristina courts - and this is in several cases in 2000 -- I'm sorry in 1997 - that several lawyers had met their clients for the first time after the investigative judge had already conducted the crucial stage of the investigation. Was this common practice in the Pristina district court?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, since we don't have it in Serbian I think it's only fair to have counsel read the precise portion from the report giving details, I mean otherwise we're mixing apples and oranges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you say to that, Ms. Carter?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just putting to the witness whether it was a common practice for lawyers to meet their clients for the first time after an investigative judge had already conducted a crucial stage of the investigation. However, I certainly can read paragraph 15 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I think it would help.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The finding: "The Special Rapporteur concludes that a number of defendants were denied an adequate defence for a variety of reasons. First, several lawyers met their clients for the first time after the investigative judge had already concluded the crucial stage of investigation, the results of which the prosecution relied upon. Lawyers experienced legal and practical difficulties obtaining access to clients at an early stage ."

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Was it common practice in the Pristina district court in 1997 to deny lawyers access to their clients until after an investigation had already concluded in that crucial stage?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that defence counsel were in communication with their clients whenever they asked for permission and whenever they found the time to visit them at the detention facility to talk to them. So I don't know what is the basis of this allegation. All that I said was so customary and it's the letter of the law that a defence counsel may visit and talk to his client in the course of preparing a defence, and there is evidence of that because every visit is recorded by the detention facility, every approval given is also recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The United Nations also took concern with one of your very specific orders in paragraph 17 of this same report. In it it indicated that access to nearly all relevant trial documents was denied to defence lawyers until shortly before the start of the trial, leaving them insufficient time to prepare a defence. "On 14 February 1997, the investigative judge of the district court in Pristina, Ms. Danica Marinkovic, made the following ruling to all applicable persons and their defence lawyers. She ruled that, for reasons of state security: 'All documents and records, as well as objects gathered as evidence and presence in certain stages of investigations, namely during the examination of the indicted and the confrontation and examination of witnesses, will be denied to the defence.' In practice, the order prohibited defence lawyers from having access to any trial documents other than the statement made by their own client to the investigative judge" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please read more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: -- "and also prevented them -- prevented their being present during the investigation of other accused persons. Consequently, access to any statements by the co-accused or essential documentary evidence for the preparation of a defence was only granted to the defence about one or at most two weeks before the start of trial." Was that common practice that defence counsel were only allowed to have a complete court file two weeks before they went to trial?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether it was two weeks, three weeks, or a month, I really can't remember, but there are legal delays envisaged by the Law on Criminal Procedure within which the defence counsel have the right to prepare after the indictment is brought and becomes valid. My colleagues and I abided by these dead-lines, so the defence counsel had the opportunity to prepare themselves. This decision was only provisional and was in force only until the end of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You remember that this particular case -- or is this the illegal MUP case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's not the illegal MUP. This is 14 February 1997, it involved the group of suspects where I investigated the charges of terrorism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And this is an accurate account of the decision that was made? What was read to you was an accurate account of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's the decision that I issued at the stage of investigation, based on my legal powers.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ma'am, were you aware that at paragraph 23 it indicates that: "The apparent practice of not permitting defendants to communicate with their legal counsel in private is a clear violation of international human rights standards for a fair trial," indicates the Human Rights Committee. Within the Pristina district court was there a limitation to the concept of the right of attorney and client privileged communications?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the issuing of the indictment, defence counsel had the right to communicate with their clients in privileged communication. That privilege was guaranteed. After the indictment was issued when they had all the elements, when they knew the charges, and the evidence available.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In paragraph 24 it goes on to say that one lawyer told the United Nations observer that interrogations of virtually all defendants in this case started in the evening, when it was difficult for them to obtain the services of a lawyer. In this case, most defendants retracted in court the statements which they had previously made, often without having received legal advice before the investigative judge, on the grounds that their statements had been extracted under torture, ill-treatment, or duress. Nevertheless, the prosecution relied upon these statements as important evidence." Do you disagree with what's contained within this UN report?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, without knowing the identity of the lawyer, I don't know how she can disagree with what one lawyer said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let us hear the answer to the question, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say that things did not stand this way. I hope defence counsel will not be offended, but when the trial began defence counsel used every means possible to get away with whatever they could get away with on behalf of their clients. They had to prove that -- this claim that the statement was taken under duress, and if such an allegation was proven then the court would never base their decision on such a statement, that was provided for by the law and it was done in practice. I can say that some defence counsel attacked me during trial and the defendants got on their feet to say that it was not true. I had a specific case when the accused whom I had investigated before came to trial saying that he had a stomachache, and I gave him a pill and then in the presence of his defence counsel, the guards, the court interpreter, and all the others, I gave him a pill for the stomachache and later I asked, Are you better now? Are you feeling well enough to explain yourself? And he told his story. At trial later the defence counsel abused this fact, said I gave him a pill for some other purpose, and the accused himself got on his feet to deny what his defence counsel was saying, saying, No, the judge gave me a pill to help me with my pain. So the defence counsel can and do use everything, all the means, to defend their clients which they believe is his main job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, just give a moment, would you, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I just, Judge, wanted to ask what was the method adopted for recording statements of those who were later to be accused? How was this done? What language was used? Was this read over to him? Was his lawyer -- was this done in the presence of his lawyer? How was it done? Were the police also -- MUP also present while this statement was being recorded? Was this man brought right from incarceration into the court to record these statements which later were retracted by such and such person. Would you kindly elaborate and explain to us how did you record these statements, I mean what environment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When a person is apprehended and detained for 72 hours, he's already in a prison facility. From there, he's taken to see a judge by the guards. It is no longer the police that do that. Once he's before me, when giving his statement his attorney is present, the one the accused chose. In a great number of cases when the accused was Albanian, we had an Albanian interpreter. Since I spoke no Albanian and the defendant knew no Serbian, therefore we used interpreters to proceed. I would pose questions, the defendant would respond, and then I would dictate. My dictation would then be interpreted by the court interpreter and that is entered in the record. After the session is finished, the accused is asked whether he wants to read the notes, some of them did, others would say, I have listened to everything that was interpreted and recorded, I have no objections to make. And we end with the sentence stating that they had no objection to the procedure and it is signed by the judge, the interpreter, the defendant, and the reporter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: What about his lawyer, did he also sign it or did you record in the order the presence of the lawyer? Because you don't -- we don't find one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript reflects who is present, including the defence counsel, the prosecutor, the name of the Albanian interpreter, the name of the judge, and the reporter. Only the accused signs all of the copies. In case the way the right to appeal is waived by the counsel, in that case it is signed by the counsel himself as well, that is the legal remedy part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Does he have sufficient opportunity of engaging a counsel of his choice after those 70 -- or within those 72 hours when he's produced before you? I mean, how is he able to get a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is known immediately since relatives find counsel and attorneys come in with their powers of attorney and they say, I am this and that person's counsel, once there is a hearing scheduled to inform him so that I can come in. Anyone who chose counsel, or rather, their counsels were notified. When asked whether they would want to be represented by a counsel, the accused would have to choose from the list or maybe they have someone beforehand, and then the counsel is invited to come in. If we are unable to locate counsel that very day, everything is postponed until next day, until the counsel is present. This is all recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: And what are your basis for formulating questions that you put to the accused, on what basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a request to conduct investigation. In the request we have the factual description of the crime that the particular defendant is charged with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Carter, can you help us by indicating the issues in the indictment that all of this goes to?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honours, persecution features predominantly within the indictment. I would indicate that that's the primary objective of this line of cross-examination, that the judiciary was functioning; however, it was not being fairly assessed on -- for the Albanian defendants. And this is going to bear in mind also as to what you're dealing with for the later prosecutions and allegations made by the same individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So this is to do with Count 5, is it, which is persecution on political, racial, and religious grounds?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and it also goes to the bias of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's a -- I understand that issue and there's a limit to the time we can spend on that particular point. But on the actual case itself I have to say I find it difficult. Is there an averment that the judicial system was being used in a discriminating way?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it's generally the persecution ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, looking at the Prosecution charge, I'm not -- speaking for myself, being assisted greatly by this; however, please continue as quickly as we can.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm happy to move on to the Gornje Obrinje incident at the end of 1998. The witness spoke of it in Friday's transcript beginning at 23526.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ma'am, you indicated in Friday's testimony that you were the investigative judge assigned to the Gornje Obrinje matter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the exhumation that was supposed to be carried out in Gornje Obrinje; if that is the case, then yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Were you also assigned within your area of responsibility the areas of Golubovac, yes or no, is that within your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what municipality Golubovac belongs to. I'm not familiar with Golubovac. I don't know whether it was within our territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How about Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Orahovac did not fall under my competence.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How about Kleka?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Urosevac, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How about Kleka?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about Kleka for the first time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One of these answers -- at least one is confusing if not wrong. The question: "How about Urosevac was answered: 'No, Orahovac did not fall within my competence.'" But what about Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Urosevac does fall under the competence of the district court.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Is Glodjane in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you give me the name of the municipality, I might tell you. I don't know what municipality Glodjane was part of.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'll do that at the break. And how about Volujak, V-o-l-u-j-a-k?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Volujak, I think it is the district court of Pec not under our authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ma'am, with regards to the investigations that were to be conducted by the Finnish authorities, were you aware that the six locations that I have just named, all six were to be reviewed by the Finns, that's Gornje Obrinje, Golubovac, Orahovac, with an O, Kleka, Glodjane, and Volujak. Were you aware that all six of those were to be addressed by the Finns?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it was that was in Urosevac that was supposed to be done by the Finnish team. I know of Gornje Obrinje, they participated there, since we set out to the on-site investigation location together. As for Kleka, I don't know what it refers to. If you mean Klecka, then, yes, they did participate in that. I don't know about the other locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, can you find a suitable place to interrupt, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: We can interrupt here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We have to break again, Mrs. Marinkovic, for lunch this time for hour. So could you please leave the court with the usher once more and we'll see you at 1.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.46 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Judge Marinkovic, speaking of the Finnish forensic team that was invited into Kosovo, were you aware that that team was actually invited by Belgrade at the highest levels?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'd heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would like to bring up P441, generally pages 98 through 100. The six sites that I had mentioned before, those were the six sites selected for the forensics team to address, specifically the KLA or KLA atrocities at Klecka, Glodjane and Volujak and the suspected atrocities by the Yugoslav forces at Gornje Obrinje, Golubovac, and Orahovac. This actually features in a Human Rights Watch report called "a week of terror in Drenica," where it discusses this investigation. You had indicated before that you believed that you were entitled to be a part of the investigation there at Gornje Obrinje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Were you aware that in a session of the Joint Command when addressing this Finnish forensic team on October 22nd of 1998, that it indicated that a five-man monitoring group -- and this is actually at page 142 in the B/C/S and page 157 in the English, but for our purposes it indicates that: "A five-man monitoring group arrived from Finland today to investigate the situation in Kosovo and Metohija and to exhume bodies." And I highlight this: "It was ordered that the cases which are currently being processed be handed over to them." Did you hand over the case of Gornje Obrinje to the Finnish forensics team?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said about that on-site investigation that we had no time to carry one out. It was safety concerns that had prevented us. I don't know what became of those bodies. The main thing is I was not able to carry out an on-site investigation that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw something here, some sort of Joint Command. I have no idea what this is about. Did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The position is quite clear in the notes of the Joint Command meeting on the 22nd of October, 1998, there is reference to a five-man monitoring group arriving from Finland that day to investigate the situation in Kosovo and to exhume bodies, and the part that's being highlighted from the notes is it was ordered that the cases which are currently being processed be handed over to them. Now, if that's not actually in the documents, then we'll look at it; but if it is, what can your objection be to the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My objection is this: There are two questions: Does she know that there is a Joint Command, there's something written there, and then we have to look into that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, there aren't these two questions. The question has been very carefully phrased: Did you hand over the case of Gornje Obrinje to the Finnish forensics team? That's the only question that's been asked, and Mrs. Marinkovic did not answered that question, so no doubt it's going to be put again.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I reiterate my question: Did you turn over the investigation to Gornje Obrinje to the Finnish forensics team?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said the last time around, I wasn't able to carry out an on-site investigation. There were safety concerns that kept us that day from going to Gornje Obrinje and exhume the bodies there. I never managed to reach those bodies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you just please answer the question first of all, and then we can move on to the next stage. Did you hand over that case to the Finnish forensics team or did you hold onto it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there was no case to hand over for me because I'd never had a case to begin with. I never reached the bodies. That's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you didn't reach the bodies because you insisted on going and having a team of MUP officers in uniform with you, and the point's being made that if you had followed what apparently had been discussed at a meeting you would not have been involved and the investigation would have taken place. So the suggestion is that you obstructed it. And let's not beat about the bush, let's get right to the issue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, it is definitely not true that I obstructed the on-site investigation. It was those who were with the Finnish team and the OSCE people who were there that did. We'd had an agreement and we were off to this on-site investigation, and then on the way into Gornje Obrinje they stopped us and said that we could proceed no further because there's some sort of a swing gate in place there that could not be crossed and there were KLA people behind it. It was risky to go in there with the police because they would be opening fire, that's what they said, and I didn't agree to do what they were proposing. It was risky, they couldn't guarantee my safety. I refused to go with them. So secondly, I was in no position to carry out an on-site investigation without the other members of my team and the police were there to secure the scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Judge Marinkovic, I would hold out to you that this order was coming from Belgrade on the 22nd of October, 1998, several months before you attempted to arrive in Gornje Obrinje. Why were you trying to enter with anybody, given the fact that it was ordered that the cases be handed directly to the Finnish forensics team?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, I'm not sure what sort of a question this is. I had been invited by the court president even before there had been a request, a specific request, by the family of one of the damaged parties from Donje Obrinje for an investigation to take place and a request was submitted to the investigating judge of the Pristina district court. And it was the president who got in touch with the OSCE people and the Finnish team. There was a meeting that everybody attended, but I wasn't there nor had anybody told me about that, that the president spoke. He got back to me and simply informed me that on such and such a day the on-site investigation would be taking place.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: About in this investigation performed by the Finnish team, in the Human Rights Watch report it indicates within the footnote that you were actually also the investigative judge in regard to the Klecka case; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Klecka, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And at that time you were called out by the Human Rights Watch because you were interrogating two ethnic Albanian suspects in front of television cameras; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of them gave a statement in the presence of a camera, but the camera was being handled by a forensic officer and that was in my office. Under the Law on Criminal Procedure, this was perfectly legitimate as long as the suspect agreed to this procedure, the suspect being interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. I would hold out to you in this Human Rights Watch report it indicated that the Finnish team conducted the investigation at Klecka without interference from the Yugoslav government or the KLA. Were you on site when the Finnish forensics team went into Klecka?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the very first I hear of the Finnish team going there or carrying out an on-site investigation there. This is not something that I was previously aware of, and I have no idea who allowed them to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And I would also hold out to you that the Finnish team per Jan Kickert during --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's go back. You gave an answer this morning that as for Klecka, then, yes, they did participate in that, referring to the Finnish team. Are you now saying they didn't to your knowledge participate in it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They did participate after I had taken some investigative steps and after our own forensics institute had carried out an investigation concerning the human bones that had been found at Klecka, but I don't know that the Finnish team actually went there, carried out an on-site investigation, or actually launched an investigation of their own at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now, moving off of Klecka and back to Gornje Obrinje, were you aware that the Finnish forensics team had already been on site the day before you tried to go with them?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In fact, Jan Kickert testified in this case at transcript 11278, line 16, that the day before the Finnish team had gone in by themselves with no MUP, no judge, no one at all, and he goes on later to say at page 11279, 5, that there was no security risk felt whatsoever by the Finnish team, as the KLA had given their assurances and wanted the exhumation of their relatives. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The situation was interpreted for my benefit in quite a different way. When they stopped us along the road and told us not to proceed to Gornje Obrinje, they told us that there were KLA soldiers there, that there was some sort of a check-point or a swing gate and that they were unable to guarantee my safety should I to go on without them in terms of being able to carry out an on-site investigation. Secondly, I couldn't do this on my own. Thirdly, I have no idea how the Finnish team could possibly carry out an on-site investigation or investigate anything at all without the approval of a state body. They were there as observers, they were forensic experts. How they could possibly have intended to carry out an on-site investigation is entirely unclear to me because this is not in keeping with the Law on Criminal Procedure, it would have run counter to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: However, I've already held out to you in Belgrade and specifically within the Joint Command it was indicated that this case -- that it was ordered that the cases which are currently being processed be handed over to the Finnish, that that is where they got their authority to go review these sites. Are you indicating that you had no knowledge whatsoever that it was the Finns who were supposed to be processing these crime sites?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know that such a document existed and that they had been granted authorisation, but they could only go to the case files, that's all they could do to see what the investigation had been like up to that point or at any stage of the procedure at all. Having inspected those documents they would have been in a position to offer their opinion on issues that they were qualified to offer opinions on, maybe in terms of that. As for an on-site investigation, I don't think they could have received authorisation for anything like that. Under the Law on Criminal Procedure you know who is in a position to carry out an on-site investigation, who would be allowed to do that. They were foreigners, they could only be there to observe or perhaps provide an additional opinion that would complement the one that had already been provided by our own forensic experts.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: However, Jan Kickert testified in this trial at page 112 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, President, sir, I don't understand this. Look at line [as interpreted] 87, lines 3 and 4, what sort of a Joint Command are we talking about in Belgrade? I think the witness should be shown what this entire story is about. I bade my time until the witness finished answering, but I think we should go back to this, look at this, Belgrade, meeting of the Joint Command, what sort of a Joint Command is this? I have no idea what we're on about here, because that's what it says, doesn't it, lines 3 and 4, 87. I want to see that, I want to be shown that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have the document, Mr. Fila. You can research it for yourself --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I know, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The answer to the question does not require that the witness see the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but Judge -- okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you feel you're somehow or other prejudiced by this, you can ask us to allow you to cross-examine later and deal with it at that stage, but it's not appropriate to interrupt the cross-examination by Ms. Carter in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I waited until the witness finished answering, that much can be said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And indeed I'm not suggesting you were in any way impolite. I'm just suggesting that this is not the stage at which to raise the matter in the way you've raised it. You can deal with it in further examination if we allow you to do that at your request later. Thank you. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Judge Marinkovic, I would hold out further that Jan Kickert testified that his understanding of the whole procedure was that the district judge, Mrs. Marinkovic, could accompany us, but I was not aware that we would have a tail of 20 armoured vehicles and APCs and police cars. Yet, you're saying that Jan Kickert was mistaken, that it was they who were merely the invitees as opposed to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the one who was in charge and I was the one who was authorised to carry out an on-site investigation in Gornje Obrinje. I would have been had we been allowed to reach the site. They were only able to observe, to make notes, and perhaps raise additional questions. They were foreigners, after all, and no foreigner could carry out an on-site investigation, only an authorised investigating magistrate can do that or another appropriate state body. What this witness said, Jan Kickert, about the armoured vehicles being there and how many there were, there weren't armoured vehicles there at all nor were there that many, not as many as he suggests. It was not a safe area. One knew at the time that KLA members were in the area and they had taken the entire area previously. It was very risky to go there. The police were there to protect me, my team, as well as the OSCE people there. They were there to make sure that we would be safe going there and returning, all of us who set out for that particular on-site investigation. It was down to them to assess what the numbers would be that were required to head for that on-site investigation and actually secure the scene. All I can say is this: While we were still travelling we reached this point where we started discussing whether we should continue or not. We were getting into the hills. I and others realized at the time that KLA members started encircling us in their black uniforms. We had already realized by this time that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're going way beyond the -- answering the question that you've been asked. Just, please, try to deal with the questions as they are being asked. Now, tell us, please, how many vehicles were with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm certain there were no armoured vehicles. Now, vehicles, were those just plain police vehicles, maybe all-terrain vehicles, or ordinary police vehicles, how many police officers can you fit into one like that, maybe four or five, I don't know. This was not something I was paying attention to. One thing I am certain about is there were certainly definitely no armoured vehicles around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Judge Marinkovic, you had indicated in previous testimony, both on Friday and today, that in the event there's a security risk that you had the option of foregoing the on-site inspection; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the sense of giving up, but in the sense of authorising the members of the Ministry of the Interior who were already there to finish this stage of the investigation or this investigative action.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: All right. There is indication within the report at P441 and in your own testimony that there were negotiations back and forth but investigation never took place for Gornje Obrinje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Well, then if the circumstances were as you suggest that they were and the Finnish team was merely supposed to watch the investigation, why didn't you request the MUP to later go in to Gornje Obrinje and do a proper investigation?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I didn't have the powers. The security situation on the ground is something that should be assessed by the MUP and not by me as an individual, private individual, or indeed as an investigating judge. Secondly, there was supposed to be an investigation on the site of the bodies there, the exhumation of the bodies, and the MUP people were not authorised to do that in my absence.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had only been called in to secure the site, that was all. The exhumation was supposed to be carried out by investigating judge and his on-site investigation team.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So if you couldn't go you were going to disallow anybody from going to attend to these bodies?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, it wasn't about going to do something or not going to do something; it was about being able to do something or not being able to do something, were there objective reasons to proceed or not, can this investigation be carried out in a safe manner, the one that we'd set out to carry out. We had to bear the following in mind, we wanted to prevent any riots from breaking out or any incidents from happening, all of those of us who were there, because the OSCE people had told me there were KLA members in the area who were armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: However, Judge Marinkovic, I would hold out to you that the Finnish team had already been able to go on site the day before with no impediment.
