utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, for completeness for the record, which I also reflect we have had evidence to this case that the International Red Cross was -- there were some tragedies, based upon mines laid by the UCK and the trenches and the well-fortified positions in Gornje Obrinje that we have. I believe General Zivanovic's report in effect and even after several days of fighting they came -- basically the positions were re-taken, that's just for everyone's recollection. Not making any further comment, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it does amount to comment that I would suggest to you was not appropriate at this stage in the cross-examination. Please continue, Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would like to discuss the further treatment of the Finnish team, specifically that the treatment of the Finnish ambassador for human rights, that in fact the -- a plain-clothes MUP officer forcibly had his camera film removed. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that. I know that one of the members of that OSCE team had arrived there with his wife, and he was given every assistance, every form of cooperation, whatever he required, whatever questions he raised were answered. I'm not sure if we're talking about the same person, but even heard from the wife of that OSCE official, she was asking me to not proceed because it was too risky. It was his wife of all people who asked me to please not go any further.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'm going to now move on to the investigation you purported to have conducted on the Fehmi Agani. You testified in this case beginning at transcript page 23495 and going through page 23498. What are you saying today your role was with regards to this investigation?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I had been informed by the duty officers of the Pristina SUP that an unidentified male body had been found by the roadside, the first thing I asked them was whether they'd informed the duty public prosecutor and the SUP inspector who was on duty. They were off to check that, and meanwhile the inspector in charge of murder had got in touch with me and confirmed that this male body had been found, but they said they had found nothing on him that would allow for identification to be made. Since at the time neither I nor the prosecutor could actually go out and inspect this ourselves --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ms. Marinkovic, are you indicating that you were the investigative judge on this case?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the investigative judge who was on duty at the time and I was informed of that. As for the on-site investigation, as I said before, this was done by the on-site investigation team without my presence because they were authorised to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Judge Marinkovic, that's a bit odd given that in the Milosevic case at page 37921, which is here today in e-court page [sic] 3115 at page 209, you indicated, and I quote: "Linked to the Fehmi Agani case, I had nothing to do with that case, I wasn't the investigative judge." You go on to say: "I didn't compile any on-site report or anything of that kind." You later go on in reading the same document that you brought in court today at page 37 -- I'm sorry, on Friday at page 37922, lines 4 through 7, that you -- I quote: "Linked to the Fehmi Agani case, what I know is this: I know a different truth, the truth that was established by the authorised Pristina SUP and I was -- have proof and evidence of that and it was a criminal report that was filed by the SUP of Pristina." Are you indicating today, contrary to what you said in the Milosevic case, that you were an active part of this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, first I have to object to misrepresentations of the record by Ms. Carter. It was actually in the prior question where she indicated that she was informed immediately after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I probably should have mentioned that as well at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This will not take long, but while there's an objection to a question we have to deal with it as a matter of law and it's appropriate in this case that we should do so without you present. So could you briefly please leave the courtroom. Just go with the usher. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the door to close, Your Honour. With respect to -- I have lost the line number, but the testimony the other day was not that she was involved in the investigation, that she was the duty judge, which she just repeated today, and that the investigation was undertaken by the police officers. I just wanted to make sure that something's not being taken out of context because the evidence that was presented through this witness the other day showed that at first the -- what's now called the Fehmi Agani case was an unknown -- an unknown --um -- unknown body that was later identified identified as Fehmi Agani as -- I don't know whether that changes anything the witness will say or not, that's just a comment that I wanted to bring to your attention, since the document for the -- I think it's 6D -- it's a 6D defence number starts off with an NN body that was discovered, and I don't know at what point in time it became Fehmi Agani. So to call something the Fehmi Agani case you have to be very specific with the dates I think. I don't know, maybe the witness can handle what Ms. Carter has given her, but if not then I would ask that the documents be shown to her and that the dates be very specific in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you say is the misrepresentation of the record? It's a quote as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Not this part, Your Honour. The misrepresentation was from the prior question where she said she investigated the scene, whereas both yesterday and today she was clear that she received the phone call and was unable to go out into the terrain and that the police officer, she even mentioned his name, was the individual who actually conducted the on-site -- the on-site investigation. And the case file on that -- on the unknown body that became Fehmi Agani for the Court's information is 6D142, so that -- if it becomes necessary, we can pull it up. I don't want to obviously lead Ms. Carter's questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Carter, you may have to repeat some of that for the witness, I'm not sure, but we see nothing wrong in the way in which you were actually posing the question so we will repel the objection. Please have the witness back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That matter's been dealt with, Mrs. Marinkovic. We can now proceed and we wish you to answer the question. If you need it repeated, then Ms. Carter will repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Do you need me to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly. You testified today when I asked you just a few moments ago that you were the investigative judge on duty and that you were responsible for the Fehmi Agani case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in charge. I was just the one who was informed that there was a body lying by the road. When I received that call, I didn't know who it was about, I didn't know the identity of the person found.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Were you the investigative judge of the case that was eventually identified as the Fehmi Agani case?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to that case, I as the investigative judge gave the order to perform a post mortem at the Institute of Forensic Medicine because the cause of death was suspicious and only a pathologist was able to tell us the truth of the matter, and that was the role I performed as the investigative judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And I hold out to you, ma'am, that when speaking of this very same matter in the Milosevic case, there at page 37921 you indicated, I quote: "Linked to the Fehmi Agani case, I have nothing to do with that case. I wasn't the investigative judge." You go on to say: "I didn't compile any on-site report or anything of that kind." How is it that when you testified in the Milosevic case you claimed no involvement with the Fehmi Agani case, yet today you sit here saying that you were the investigative judge and became highly involved in that case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I hate to do this, but I think -- I don't want to be accused of influencing the witness by my objection. So if we could just briefly have her out again. I think it relates -- well, I don't want to say too much more with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, do you know any English? Do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Will you take your headphones off, please, while we discuss this. Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's much more efficient. We spent a great deal of time going through the various steps of an investigative judge, including an investigation and an on-site investigation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, before you go any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is the lady who has personal knowledge of the extent to which she was or was not involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: She's the person we would expect to be able to distinguish between being the investigative judge at the NN stage and being the investigative judge at the point when the body is later identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the investigative judge goes out for the "uvidjaj" or on-site investigation, it is different from the investigative judge that does the investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Equally, she should be the person who is most equipped to be able to make that distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree. I just know that in the past the two words "uvidjaj" on-site investigation and investigation have been inter-mixed. So I don't know what the original Serbian was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you will have an opportunity to re-examination on anything that's unclear as a result of her answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. We've dealt with that matter and we can now proceed with the evidence. Ms. Carter. Ms. Carter wants to know why in Milosevic you said that you had -- you were not the investigative judge and is asking you to explain the difference -- the apparent difference between what you said in that case and what you've said so far in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said at the Milosevic trial was that as the investigative judge I didn't conduct the investigation because the investigation, as investigation, implies a pre-indictment proceedings where we know who the perpetrator is and what the crime is. In the Agani case, the only thing I did as the investigative judge was to issue an order for a post mortem to be done, which doesn't mean that an -- I conducted the investigation. It is just one of the investigative steps. The investigating judge has to issue the order for a post mortem to be performed. That's the only thing I did in that case. That was my only participation. After that we know that a criminal report was filed and that report was shown to me when I testified in the other case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Judge Marinkovic, I would hold out to you that these distinctions were not drawn by you or by anybody in the Milosevic case, and in fact you were being presented with some statements about you said by Natasa Kandic and you, sua sponte said, linked to the Agani case: "I have nothing to do with case, I wasn't the investigative judge."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I hope this is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the fact that in another proceeding no one asked questions to investigative --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sit down. You're just interfering with the cross-examination now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Your Honour. I think this is a very important point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I want it on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sit down and deal with it in re-examination. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I will begin at page 37920 which brought this to my attention. The question asked to you by Mr. Nice in regards to the Natasa Kandic statements was: "Let's look at the article then for that. What's more important is the rest of what she was able to complain about. If this can be placed on the overhead projector, please. It's an article of the 8th of March, 2002, a publication of that date, and it says that you, "Formally investigative judge of Pristina district court, reacted to the Humanitarian Law Centre press release on the murder of Fehmi Agani and accused Natasa Kandic of lying." Did you accuse her of lying? Your answer was: "Let me tell you this: I'm surprised that you're using as a source of information complaints about my work and that for that you have used Natasa Kandic as a source. For me as an individual, well, I don't know her. She's not interesting as far as I'm concerned. I would like you to tell me specifically in concrete terms the complaints made against my work" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please read more slowly when reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're being asked to read more slowly, but I at the moment do not see the purpose of this narrative.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am about to get to the exact quote that we are arguing about with Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: It says: "I would like you to tell me specifically in concrete terms the complaints made against my work, whether the parties involved in the proceedings themselves in the investigation themselves that complained about me not this source." And then you were asked again: "Did you accuse her of lying." And your response to that question was: "Linked to your question I have concrete proof that I can put before the Trial Chamber. Linked to the Fehmi Agani case, I have nothing to do with this case. I wasn't the investigative judge." So when you responded in that manner in the Milosevic case, there was no indication that you were investigative judge of some or all of this investigation. You flat out declared that Natasa Kandic was a liar and that you were not the investigative judge. How can you then sit here today and indicate that you were involved in this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, first of all, could you tell me, Ms. Carter, what Natasa Kandic said? What is the accusation?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the record in the Milosevic case that was presented this is just that she -- that she had been the subject of many complaints in the course of her work, and Natasa Kandic at 37919 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What were the complaints? Give us a specific example of a complaint that she was making as -- I mean, I entirely understand why Mrs. Marinkovic wanted to know what the complaints were.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thought I was put it on the ELMO, so it ought to have been marked as some sort of an exhibit in the Milosevic case as well. I don't know if we can get that on such short notice.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If it was, it was not noted as an exhibit number, so I'm not sure what was presented. However, my understanding is that there was a question about Mrs. -- I'm sorry, Judge Marinkovic's involvement within the Agani case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, your -- all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Because the article that was being presented --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we don't know what the complaint was, right. Now, where are we? I mean, you've asked repeatedly this question about being investigative judge. What is the specific point you want to put rather than just giving us narratives of what other people have said that's of no value to the progress of this trial?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Specifically, Your Honour, that this witness has either perjured herself in the Milosevic case or she is perjuring herself now. She was very clear about what her role was there, and I would argue to the Court that by her sitting here today and on Friday and discussing all of the lovely investigation that was done on this case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll hear the speeches later. What is the specific question?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How does Mrs. --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Judge Marinkovic, how is -- are both statements true, that in Milosevic you indicated that you were not the investigative judge and you had nothing to do with it; however, you sit here today and say that you were the investigative judge and had quite a bit to do with it? How do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you see, that's a mis-characterization of today's evidence. Why do you need to go over the whole narrative again? Why can't you ask pointed questions and then we'll work out what the sum and substance of the evidence is? She's made it clear that her only role was to arrange for a post mortem, that was it. Now, if you say that's a lie, put it to her and see what she has to say, and put it on the basis before that she said before she had nothing to do with the case at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Judge Marinkovic, I'll ask you in the way Judge Bonomy has just stated. How is it that in the Milosevic case you indicate that you had nothing to do with this case whatsoever, yet you sit here today indicating that you have ordered post mortems and any other activity that you had?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only repeat the answer I've already given. The investigation in that case was not conducted because the perpetrator was unidentified and there was nothing for me to do as the investigative judge, and it's correct that I had no participation in the investigation. As for the post mortem, it's just one of the investigative steps which in that moment was ordered alongside the on-site investigation, to collect the evidence, to be available for one day when the perpetrator is found.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is counsel going to be withdrawing the comments about perjury because those are very serious comments coming from a Prosecution that has brought several witnesses who signed sworn statements that are contrary to their evidence on very key issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I don't make those accusations, and I think that they are very serious accusations to be made with no support.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber's going to adjourn just briefly and we will resume in ten minutes or so, about quarter to. So there's no point in everyone standing down. The accused should stay where they are, counsel may be free to move around. Just let us have an opportunity to consider this situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: --- Break taken at 2.35 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, do you want to respond to what Mr. Ivetic said?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, I based my -- the way I responded to -- made that statement to the Court because we've already been told that you can't use the word "liar" or "lying," or anything like that, unless we're going to use Mr. Hannis's suggestion as an unconvicted liar. This would be -- they said at the time we were having this argument, that to call somebody a liar you had to be convicted of perjury. So I'm trying to simply abide by the extreme dislike on the Defence bar in saying that somebody is lying or speaking an untruth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I didn't realize we had made any specific rulings on the matter. I think it was a question of being sensitive to different perceptions based on culture or legal practice that might lead to someone being offended by a remark in a way that that -- a person in another country would not be offended. And what happened in this instance was that the statements were made as an explanation of the Prosecution position rather than in the context of a question, and that has led Mr. Ivetic to say, Well, that should be withdrawn, it wasn't there as a question, it was a submission. Well, Mr. Ivetic, we take the view that it was an explanation of the Prosecution position rather than something that we in any way have approved. We sought that explanation, we got it, and no doubt we'll have an opportunity to resolve it if necessary at the end of the case. I think Judge Marinkovic understands that the practice here is somewhat different from the practice in her own jurisdiction and indeed others with which her jurisdiction might be compared, but it's quite common in this jurisdiction for the assertion to be made that either one statement must be a lie or the other must be a lie. And we as lawyers get used to that sort of thing. We appreciate when in the witness box that that may happen, but until a court makes a pronouncement to that effect it's simply part and parcel of the procedure that's adopted in challenging evidence. So we do not propose to take any action on this matter, Mr. Ivetic. We note the feeling with which you will no doubt address the matter in due course, and that you are giving us clear notice of what you will in due course say. Mr. Fila, do you have any questions you wish authority -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Judge Chowhan's anxious I make it clear to you, as I thought I was making clear, Mrs. Marinkovic, that we make no judgement on what the Prosecution are saying at this stage. We will deal with that later once we've heard all the evidence and all the arguments, and you can rest assured we will be sensitive to your position in the whole matter and indeed to the way in which you've addressed the questions that have been posed in cross-examination. Now, Mr. Fila, do you have questions you wish to ask rather than assertions you wish to make that bear a very close resemblance to assertions you have made on many occasions already in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm just trying to be helpful, and I certainly don't want to contradict Ms. Carter. So what's my position? There's the person called Radomir Lukic a famous lawyer in our country, an academician, and he claims that 90 per cent of any sort of discussion that goes on between lawyers is purely technological. I've been listening to the word investigation the whole day today, whenever I'm raising it because of this damned investigation. In your system an investigation is any sort of check; in our country investigation is something that is very precisely and strictly defined. This is something that is done by the investigating magistrate, and it contains the name and family name of a suspect and it states in no uncertain terms what he's suspected of and then there must be a decision by the investigating magistrate. That's all I'm trying to say. As for this other thing I've been saying. In P1468, that's an exhibit, and these are the notes of the Joint Command, the 22nd of November, 1998, page 142 in e-court, there is evidence by Mijatovic where he says that a group of Finnish forensic experts would be there to do some work. It doesn't say anywhere that this is an order from Belgrade, as Ms. Carter suggests. Secondly, it doesn't say anywhere that there will be an investigation because now I'm going back to the first thing that I said, because in our country we can't let someone else run an investigation who is not a judge, but I have to double-check your own meaning of the term investigation. They've got to look at that, they've got to be handed a case, they've got to be handed a post mortem. So that's your investigation, it's not the same sort of investigation that the witness is referring to. That's the second distinction. The third distinction: No notes from the Joint Command from Belgrade exist. There.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You need to be fair, though, Mr. Fila, to Ms. Carter as well. What she was submitting or what she was saying is contained in the minute of that meeting is a statement that the Finns were to take the lead basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No -- yes, misinterpreted. This has been misinterpreted. It has been entirely misinterpreted. Somebody should read this in the Serbian. You see, you'll get another translation too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we have the page on the screen, please, it's P1468 --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objection to this. I would also note for the court --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think Mr. Fila was saying page 142 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And just to point out for the record, Your Honour, that we've already gone through this exercise at page 22231 with witness Stakic, however, if we want to go through it an additional time, that's fine, but the translation was confirmed on that date, that's on 12th February 2008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that the correct English -- well, which person made the remark, Mr. Fila said Mijatovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic is that one who is: "Is attributed to within the Joint Command notes" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which page in English?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: It's in page 157 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it might be a good idea for someone to read this in the Serbian original. It's very difficult, you know, that's why I put this on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not hear the last word.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "I was ordered to give them -- ordered -- today -- today one -- today came one group of five from Finland for verifying the situation in Kosovo and Metohija, for exhuming the bodies. They were ordered to be handed over cases that are already being processed about" -- what's it say? Sorry? Yes, that's that. "Ordered to be handed over cases that are being processed." It doesn't say anywhere that they were given the right to carry out any investigations in our sense of the word. In your sense of the word, to have a look, yes. That's why I'm saying that all we're having is a terminological debate between Ms. Carter and the Defence because you see where it says: "They were ordered to be handed over" -- not for the case to be handed over to them entirely, but for them to inspect these cases that are being processed were, for them to have a look, not to actually be in charge of the cases. It's not possible under the Law on Criminal Procedure, and I think this applies to each country that I know of. So that is the essence of what I am saying. And they came there for the exhumation of the bodies, not for the investigation, not to run an investigation. So this is a purely terminological thing you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think I understood it any differently from the way you're explaining, Mr. Fila, but the Prosecution response to that would be of course as soon as you combine it or try to combine it with the on-site investigation or any formal element of the investigation and insist on the presence of uniformed police officers, then the end result may be to thwart the Finnish efforts. That's all that's being said at the moment and that's something we'll have to review in its context in due course. It's a constant issue, as you know, with terrorism all over the world that when you try to carry out a check on what's going on someone will have a point of view that may obstruct the efforts to get at the truth and they may be right. They may have right on their side, but right does not necessarily mean in this situation that you'll establish the truth. So it's always a delicate exercise in the end to try to find a way through the complications that are created by warring parties where one might regard the other as a terrorist and the other might regard himself as a freedom fighter.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, it was not my intention to offend Ms. Carter, and there's something else. Until there's formal solution on a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sure you failed even if it was your effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I never made an effort to do that, God forbid. And then allow me to go on. Perhaps this would be a good thing to know. Until there is a formal decision that there should be an investigation, and this is something that is done by a judge, we call all of this pre-criminal proceedings in our country and then it suddenly starts making sense, finally. Could Ms. Carter please show what these notes are from Belgrade that she showed the witness. Mrs. Marinkovic, these are Joint Command notes from Belgrade talking about the Finnish forensic experts. I'd like to hear about it, it may be something that I missed during this trial. I think that's actually stated on the record. This might be a mistake. If that indeed is the case, I'll just forgot about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it, Ms. Carter, what you are referring to is what Mr. Mijatovic is recorded as saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I actually do now understand what the objection of Mr. Fila is. When we first began the exercise, I asked the witness if she was aware of direction from Belgrade allowing the Finnish team to come in, and I later asked for the Joint Command and so I think those two things might have gotten confused. She has indicated that she knew it from Belgrade. The Joint Command minutes are obviously held in Pristina, but they are speaking of the same team coming in to do the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's as far as we can take this matter, Mr. Fila. Thank you very much for your assistance. Re-examination, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll be very brief. I thought one other colleague had something he wanted to raise before I -- then I will begin. I guess that's -- I have moot information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Judge Marinkovic, I will be brief and then we will be finished with you today. The first question I would like to ask of you is: Are there circumstances within the Serbian -- the Serbian judicial system wherein the investigative judge is not utilised but rather prosecutors can proceed directly upon criminal reports or criminal denunciations, so we're on the same page, and directly raise indictments based upon those filings?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the Law on Criminal Procedure, that situation is envisaged as well. The public prosecutor, pursuant to a criminal report and based on the dates -- data contained therein as well as its annexes, can raise an indictment without a previous investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. And I used the break to go back to the transcript to see the exact wording of the exchange regarding Fehmi Agani because I thought I was going to be able to get rid of one of my questions, but unfortunately the wording is not as precise as I would like it to be. Now, with respect to the -- what's been called the Fehmi Agani case. At the time that you issued a request for a post mortem, had the body been identified or was it an NN, or unidentified, case of which there were many -- I don't know, probably hundreds of thousands in your career?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment I issued a request for a report, post mortem, it was an unidentified male corpse. It is only at the forensic institute that the forensic experts established the identity and carried out a post mortem.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And again, Your Honours, for the record, 6D142 has already been exhibited, so I'm not going to go through it again. That's the whole file on the "Fehmi Agani" case which shows what the first paperwork was with respect to an unknown body.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Moving on to my other set of questions. Judge Marinkovic, in the course of interviewing ethnic Kosovo Albanians in the course of your work, when -- did you have occasion to come across Albanian -- Kosovo Albanians that spoke the Serbian language; and if so, what was the name in Serbian that they used to describe their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had occasion to see some individuals who appeared before me either as a defendant or the injured party that they knew Serbian and could speak it well; however, it was during the time when I worked in litigation, in civil law. And parties would appear. We would take down their data, and when inquiring about their ethnicity they would use the word "Siptar." They didn't mind to use it. It was a standard term. It was not pejorative. I can tell you of a colleague of ours who was Albanian. We all called him "Siptar" when not using his name. We use it with a degree of sympathy. It wasn't pejorative at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm trying to find the exhibit and I'm having a hard time, but I don't need to focus on the exhibit. Hopefully I can describe it in enough detail. There was talk during Madam Carter's cross-examination about a UN report which actually, as I recall, was authored by one individual, Ms. Sophie [sic] Rehn or Stephanie [sic] Rehn [sic] as Special Rapporteur for the UN. And the question I have -- I actually have two questions for you in that regard. Did anyone from the United Nations subsequent to -- pardon -- let's back up. Did anyone from the United Nations prior to publishing this report contact either yourself or the president of the court or anyone else for that matter to conduct an official inquiry into the court records to verify any of the claims that are set forth therein?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one talked to me about it. This is the first time I hear that there was a UN representative at the district court in Pristina. Had that person talked to the president of the court, the president would have checked those allegations with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I take it then that no one asked you to -- asked either you or the president of the court to confirm any of the allegations contained in the -- in the piece after it had been published?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one, no one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And my last question might be redundant given your answer at page 113, 16, that was the first time you heard about a UN representative. Did you or anyone else at the Pristina court receive a copy of this report at any point in time, and I apologise, I believe the date was 1997 -- 1996 or 1997 for the Court, I don't have it in front of me, but at any point in time after it was published did you ever receive a copy of the same from either the author, Ms. Stephanie Rehn I think it is or from the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was never given a copy of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, unless you have some further questions for Judge Marinkovic, I'm finished my re-direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Judge Marinkovic, I thank you for your time and patience and I apologise for keeping you here over the long weekend, but it was necessary for the interests of justice for truth to come out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming here again to give evidence and to assist the Tribunal. You may now leave the courtroom with the usher. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to thank Their Honours for treating me fairly. I understand the conduct of the Prosecutor, since it is their work, but when I go back to Kragujevac my colleagues are waiting for me impatiently to learn of the actual work of this Tribunal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had intended to have Mr. Pantic as our next witness, but he arrived on Sunday afternoon and I had been actually bedridden for the last two days with antibiotics and codeine, so I did not finish preparing him and the witness that Mr. Lukic was preparing after him is almost finished but not quite finished. So we beg the Court's indulgence. I did mentioned to Mr. Haider. I know we have the hearing scheduled for later this afternoon, if no one has any objection and if it works out for the Court we could advance to this time and perhaps give everyone some time this afternoon for other pressing personal matters or something of the like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will need a break, though, that's the problem. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. Well, my lead counsel is -- wanted to be present at the hearing so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that was scheduled for 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we can't really advance that if having announced the time those involved are intending to rely upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I was just trying to be helpful. I see now looking at the clock that even with the break we wouldn't make it until after 4.00. So I would suggest that with Your Honour's leave that we adjourn until the 4.00 hearing and either Mr. Lukic or I will be hear for that to participate. As I understand, it's primarily a ruling or -- one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry, there's some communication between the counsel as to when Mr. O'Sullivan is going to be here and Mr. Ackerman as well. I think with that doubt in mind, we should probably keep the regularly scheduled time so that there's no unexpected absences and that everyone is properly represented at that very important hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What we'll do then is adjourn until 4.00

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is a procedural hearing at which we're anxious to hear from the parties on certain miscellaneous issues largely connected with the final stages of the case. I note that three of the accused are present and three are not. Mr. Ackerman, Mr. Pavkovic is not here. I take it he's content that this hearing proceeds in his absence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, he chose not to be here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, can the same be said of Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Ivetic, the same be said about Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's my understanding and I think the original hearing said that clients may need not be present, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but I'm just anxious to see that we proceed with his approval in his absence with his approval. What I think we'd like to do first of all is hear from the Prosecution from Mr. Hannis. The only particular development to note I think was that parties had an opportunity of discussing the programme of events towards the end of the trial process with Mr. Dawson at the request, I think, of the Defence but with the approval of the Bench. Having heard what was said then, we thought it only right that the issues discussed should be discussed with the Bench in open court, and that was the main reason for holding this hearing. So, Mr. Hannis, do you wish to make any proposals in relation to these final stages of the trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there were a couple things. In the meeting we had with Mr. Dawson, I think the Defence counsel went first and set forth the time-period that they thought they needed and would like to have between the close of evidence and the filing of the final briefs. And I think their time-period they asked for was three months, and I, I guess, trying to be more macho said that the Prosecution intended only to ask for two months, but I couldn't disagree with them that three months might be an appropriate amount of time. Your Honours, I think there is a big pile of evidence in this case and I think it would be helpful to you if the parties have a substantial period of time to try and organize that and present it to you in a coherent fashion. I could spend a few weeks just reading Joint Command meetings and VJ collegium meetings and MUP meetings. There's a lot to be gleaned from that documentary evidence and some of it frankly I'm still trying to get ahold of. So I guess that's where we are. One question I had, I think I raised it with Mr. Dawson, was we did not know whether the Court had any present intention of calling its own witnesses or seeking any additional evidence and maybe it's too early to make that inquiry because you may not know the answer to that until you've heard everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there may be a limited number of Chamber witnesses and we will obviously need to deal with that in the fairly near future, identifying them and determining the procedure to be followed, but I would not envisage hearing them taking a significant period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I don't see that taking a significant period of time, but it factors into our calculation of how much time we need from the close of all the evidence until the written briefs are done. And now we know, if there are no additional witnesses from the Court, we know sort of universe of witnesses and documents from which we'll be writing. But if the Court calls some witnesses, depending on who they are and what they talk about, that could have some impact on that, that's reason why I mention that. I don't have anything further for you other than, you know, we will make our best efforts to comply with whatever time-period you set upon us. I know that sounds like a long period of time, but there is a lot of evidence in this case and I think for us to be helpful to you we would benefit from that amount of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On the other hand, we have been in court for a long time, parties in presenting their case have to have in mind the framework of what they're trying to establish or alternatively what they're trying to undermine. And some would say that before you can conduct a meaningful trial you need to know what your closing arguments are. So we have indicated I think a number of times that we expected the final briefs to be a work in progress as the case progressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on our side, Your Honour, it has been and we have finished with our Prosecution phase of the case a long time ago. We have been able to marshal that evidence and put it in our working closing brief, but as I think I've said in the past and I know Your Honours understand that evidence is a living, breathing thing, and it changes in this case -- in some cases, in some instances every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One other possibility of course is that you seek rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you able to help us on that at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As I stand here today, I don't foresee that. I mean, there are individual issues and small items, but I don't see some big solid kind of thing that we feel like we need to address or that we have a rebuttal case to put to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We don't anticipate asking for that at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, to just pick up on the meeting we had with Mr. Dawson, another matter that arose was a suggestion on our part to stagger the time of filing the briefs and have in essence -- give us an opportunity to see the final Prosecution brief in an attempt to stream-line the respective Defence briefs. Now, if -- I'm not sure whether Mr. Hannis considers two months a substantial period or whether he wants more for his substantial period, but if he can do it in less than three months, we'll gladly take those extra 30 days to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not a practice that I think's been followed in this Tribunal to stagger the submission of these final briefs on the basis that the closing arguments are a suitable occasion to respond to issues that you feel need to be addressed further.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I believe there's precedence both ways, Your Honour. In some Chambers they have, the Celebici case for example, in other cases they have not. So there's room there for whatever if the Chamber so choses. I think that this case, and I think there's general agreement on our side of the room, that this very long trial has gone very efficiently because we've sat full weeks and long days. And so this trial in fact has been much shorter in relative terms than the way cases are conducted by other Trial Chambers. But one consequence of being in court as much as we are is that we do not have as much time out of court to work on submissions. I'm fully aware of your remarks that of course throughout the course of the trial we have been marshalling evidence and analysing it. I believe the Chamber should also bear in mind that the extensive use of 92 ter makes analysis of any individual witness that much more labour-intensive. A tremendous amount of bar table submissions are coming recently and probably more will come from both Ojdanic and Lazarevic and Lukic. A lot of evidence has been coming in on paper as we work our way through the remainder of the live witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you involved in the Celebici case, Mr. O'Sullivan?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In that case you, no doubt, sat longer days than you've been sitting in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Those were days when mornings and afternoons were regularly used by one trial; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We also had -- it was two weeks -- it was two or three weeks on and two or three weeks off also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: While you did another case.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: There was one courtroom in those days and two trials.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was there too, there was one courtroom and we were sharing it with another case. So we would sit for two weeks of full days and then they would sit for two weeks full days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How long did the evidence in the case actually --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you mind slowing down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: A year?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I believe it started in March of 1997 and finished in the summer of 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And it was quite a big case?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Four accused, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It -- I to some extent may be sounding defensive, Mr. O'Sullivan, but when you do look back this case is perhaps not quite as unique as has been suggested at times in the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, if you're not sounding defensive, I don't want to sound offensive, but the Celebici case was primarily a camp case where -- with guards and it was not document-intensive except for one accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And this case, of course, is quite the opposite, regardless of the fact we do benefit from electronic software and equipment. And I also think that so much will also depend on rebuttal, rejoinder, and Court witnesses. Now, those are perhaps more obvious variables at this stage based on what Mr. Hannis and what the Chamber has said, but regardless there's just an enormous amount of material that all the parties must digest and address, partly because of the fact the way the indictment's framed we have to peruse all the evidence, every accused has to. Now, my colleagues may have more specific submissions in their respective cases, but I think that's the gist of what we discussed among ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis, do you have -- I should have asked you about the idea of staggering the submission of the briefs. Do you have anything to say on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just that we were opposed to it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, do you have submissions to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have arguments that I have personally want to submit. When I write a 200-page submission, I would like you not to force me to read what I've already submitted because this is a practice that I really don't like before this Tribunal. Once you receive something, then I have to argue it orally. This is something that I find quite offensive, both for me and for you. If I have anything to add to it because I will see Mr. Hannis's submission at a later stage or somebody else's submission. So then I may have to add something, but this is something that I have to admit this is where I am lazy. I would like to ask you not to force me to do that. I would like to be given a chance merely to respond to Mr. Hannis. This is all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, you'll be punished by us if you endeavour to read something you've already written which we can read for ourselves. But the issue really is whether the final briefs are all filed simultaneously or whether they should be staggered. Now, it's not clear to me which version -- which idea you're supporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I am always in favour of any concepts that are detrimental to the Prosecutor, and in this case that would be the 30-day dead-line, after all I am a Defence counsel and this would be something that would be better for me, but I'm not sure if it would be better for Mr. Hannis. But I do agree with that idea and then our closing arguments could be even shorter because then the response to Mr. Hannis would already be incorporated in our briefs and then you could limit us to one hour for our closing arguments, that would be quite sufficient. And I agree that the Prosecutor should then be given more time to respond, that would be only fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to add something very briefly, follow-up to what Mr. O'Sullivan has said. The way we understand the procedure so far, and unlike other cases before this Tribunal, we've been trying to cut short the trial time in courtroom. That is why so many of us have submitted so many bar table motions for admission of evidence from the bar table, that's one thing; and on the other hand it's been stressed so many times during this trial that some things will be explained at a later stage in our submissions, that we will be given an opportunity to explain some things through some documents and briefs. And if you go back to the transcript, if you do a search you will see that this is something that's been repeated quite often. And at the end we face a situation where we see the light at the end of the tunnel. We can now see the end to our time in the courtroom, but we really don't have enough time or either we're asking to be given enough time to analyse all those things that happened outside the courtroom in this case. And this is really the biggest difference between this case and the other cases before this Tribunal. So far in all the cases including the ancient cases such as Celebici and so on, most of the evidence was admitted in the courtroom; and this new rule really made it impossible for us to get the full picture of what has been admitted from the bar table on the part of the other Defence teams and sometimes on the part of the Prosecution because they had some quite substantial submissions of this kind. So this is the main reason why we asked to be given more time, to be able to deal with all that, to process all that. Unfortunately, given the pace of our trial, we have been given very little time to deal with that. So this is the time that we, at least I'm speaking for myself and for my Defence team, we're asking to be given enough time to analyse the documents that were admitted in this manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I suppose I have two matters I want to touch at least a little bit on. I've been here for over ten years now and I've seen a lot of cases go by here, and I think, Your Honour, you have accomplished something in this case that has never happened in this Tribunal before, and that is you have managed to take an extraordinarily complicated case and compress it into a pretty small bit of time. And I say that by referring to the longer days that we've spent in trial week after week, to the extensive use of 92 ter which has never been used to that extent before that I know of in a case, and the extremely extensive use of bar table admissions. And that's resulted in a -- in a body of evidence that if someone were to analyse it I think would find that on a per-day basis it just vastly exceeds anything that's ever happened in this Tribunal before. That has -- that has I think worked to the definite advantage of this Tribunal in terms of moving this case fairly rapidly through the process. We now get to a point where we need to try to present to you the best that we can do with regard to what this all means, all this evidence that's been going on and coming on in various ways. There are documents that are part of the evidence in this case that I know some of us haven't seen yet, documents coming from the bar table just recently and that will come from the bar table at the end of the Lukic case. We have no idea what those will be or whether once that happens there might be some need to deal with those in some way. We don't know that. In any event, the body of evidence that needs to be dealt with here is significant, and I wouldn't suggest for a moment that we haven't been working quite hard on trying to marshal that together and make some sense of it and start putting together a brief. You've seen me not being here very much and that's because that's what I've been doing. But in the process of trying to do that one keeps getting distracted by things that are going on here everyday, motions that are filed that you need to respond to, requests from the Court that you need to respond to, bar table things that are filed that you try to figure out and read. It's very hard spending your day sitting in the office working on the final brief when the trial is going on and things are happening that are distracting you away from that. And to do any kind of a decent job of assisting Your Honours with a final brief, it needs to be done at a time when you are not distracted by other matters that are going on, when you can actually sit down and think about it and put some brain power into it. With regard to when briefs are filed, it seems to me logic would suggest this. The burden of proof in this case is on the Prosecution, so they should file their brief taking their best shot based on the evidence there is; and we should then, because we do not have a burden, we should then have an opportunity to respond to that brief and present our best case. That way you'll get the most efficient brief from the Defence. It will not then be briefs that are trying to anticipate where the Prosecution might be going to go, but briefs that are directed to the issues that the Prosecution believes are worthy of briefing to you. It might be in fairness to the Prosecution then that upon the filing of the Defence briefs that they have a short period of time to reply to those because they would be replying to the Defence positions that are not necessarily replies to the Prosecution position. And in the view of the law requiring the Prosecution to prove the case beyond a reasonable doubt, that seems to be a very logical way to do it, and I would strongly recommend that it be done that way. There is no precedent in this Tribunal that would send you in either direction; you're free to choose what you think is the most logical and best way to do that. And I'm suggesting to you that I think what I just suggested may very well be it. I know that it sounds at first blush rather excessive to say we need three months to do this, but when you look at the enormous body of evidence there is here to deal with, I don't think it is. I think it's reasonable, I think it's very reasonable, especially when you consider that we don't have the kind of a staff that -- one of the biggest cases ever tried in the United States was the IBM case, for instance, there were 25 lawyers I believe who worked on that case. We don't have that kind of luxury here. We have to deal with very small staffs and we try to deal with this huge body of evidence with nowhere near as many people as a normal case would have working on it. I can also understand why Mr. Hannis would think two months would be sufficient because, as you know, they do have more people than we have. They have a larger staff to work on things, they have people that are out working on this case every day, and Mr. Hannis will agree with that. I know that they feel like they don't have enough people, but you just look at the number of lawyers that troop in here representing the Prosecution, there's a lot more than we have. I know you're looking at him like you're going to respond to this, aren't you Mr. Hannis. But it's true, Judge, it's absolutely true. They do have more people. We just don't have that kind of a staff. So I think our requests are reasonable, I think they should be granted, and I think you'll be pleased with the quality of work you'll get if you do give us the time to do the job that we're all capable of doing if we have the time to do it, and I think our clients would be happy if we were given the chance to represent them to the best of our abilities. I think that would be helpful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In case it's of any interest to anyone, I have been given the information that in Celebici the Defence briefs -- well, at least three of them were filed three days after the Prosecution brief and one a bit later, another three days later. I don't know if there is any other precedent, other than for simultaneous filing. However, it's an interesting proposition that we will have regard to. Now, Mr. Bakrac, do you want to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I agree with everything that the previous speakers said, but since you're asking me now what option would be chosen by the Lazarevic Defence team, I think that Mr. O'Sullivan's proposal to have 30 days in addition for our own filings after the Prosecutor is a reasonable one. If we file our briefs at the same time, simultaneously, we will have to have a certain number of days and enough time to prepare responses in terms of our closing arguments. At any rate, we will have to have time to respond to the Prosecutor's final brief. That is what I wish to say in relation to that matter. On behalf of General Lazarevic's Defence, I would like to note to the Trial Chamber that we have just finished presenting our own defence and now we are dealing with General Lukic's defence. You know that the fifth defence and General Lazarevic's defence has to follow actively the sixth defence's evidence, so we don't really have time now to deal seriously with the writing of our final brief. Bearing in mind the fact that the last three defences joined this case at a later date, our problem is simply compounded by that. I don't really want to repeat anything I have said, but I have already said that experience has always taught me that it's invariably better if you set my time rather than I speak myself. I would give myself three months' time in this particular case. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'll be brief. I think everyone has said a lot and I think, although I wasn't present at the hearing with Mr. Dawson, I understand it was very productive and a lot of issues were raised forth. The only thing I would like to stress with respect to the Lukic Defence team is that essentially we're going to be going full speed until the end of the case. So -- whereas other people could perhaps get -- the notions someone can get an early start on some of the briefs, we really will need every break and planned pause we have to complete preparations for our Defence case, especially the upcoming break to again finalise some of our non-domestic witnesses from Germany, America, Canada, Spain, et cetera. So really in essence it's -- when we say two or three months, and I think we -- with the Defence is all clear on three months, we envision that time as being from whenever the last witness is completed, be that a 6D witness, a Trial Chamber witness, or be an eventual rebuttal witness. That we believe that that time-period is the logical and reasonable one that I think we need to get the proper job done and to get the proper defence for our clients and to make a proper record. Apart from that we're always at the convenience of the Trial Chamber, and if there's any other submissions or other information that the Trial Chamber thinks following this hearing, as we have in the past we will always try to respond with specifics or if need be written or oral submissions in that regard. But such -- as I said, we're in the unique position that we have to kind of keep going at a heavy pace throughout the rest of this circuit. One thing that we're going to be trying to do to try and not wait until the last minute is I intend to file multiple bar table motions, perhaps sometimes with five or six documents or ten documents depending on what I have translated at any given point in time. I'm not going to -- I've trying to avoid mega bar table motions filed at the last -- at the 11th hour. So I hope that will help everyone in terms of the work that does need to get done from here to the end of this journey. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In your case, Mr. Ivetic, we do have a rather longer agenda I think. You've dealt to some extent with the question of bar table motion. We need some sort of sign of activity on that front or alternatively we will require ourselves to make an order in everyone's interests to get this dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Agreed. I expect to get -- we -- we should have some of the shorter bar table motions in the near future, in a matter of a week or two I think. We did have of course some motions to amend the 65 ter list that I -- that need to be before we can match the estimates they admitted via the bar table. So...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You also have to have a clear idea in your mind of the length of your case. A report on the use of time has just been filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Last Friday I think, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No yesterday I think, which indicates that you're more than halfway through the allocation of hours when we made the order. Now, as presently advised, that would suggest that your case will be over in the middle of April. I'm not sure -- this bears an uncanny resemblance to what happened with Mr. Lazarevic's case. I'm not sure that you've really worked out how you're going to deal with that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Like I said, we have a lot of other issues that are ongoing in our -- in the midst of our preparation of our case, including preparing 92 ters for some witnesses, cutting down the scope of other witnesses, and trying to do bar table motions and not necessarily go through every document with every witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Possibly number one on your list has to be how you're going to make use of your in-court time. The debate so far has largely been about out-of-court time. But if I can give you an example of the problem -- one of the problems we see here, Mr. Lazarevic in his evidence was 20 hours in chief. You have an estimate of ten hours for Mr. Lukic, you haven't got him on your latest list of witnesses for March and April, but you indicated to us last week that you hadn't made a decision about calling him. Now, are you any further forward on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Not on that, Your Honour. What we have been doing, hopefully and it's been obvious, is trying to present at the beginning of the case what we view as critical witnesses on various topics so that as we get down to some of the other witnesses that had a similar position, you know, the border crossing at Djeneral Jankovic or something, they will not be as extensive as the first witness on the border crossings issue. But we felt that we needed to cover some basic ideas about the operation and functioning, particularly because there has been so much confusion even back in the day, in 1998 and 1999, about how exactly the MUP operated, as I think has been apparent from some of the testimony and some of the military documents, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm looking at something a bit more fundamental than that at the moment. It may be that we would require to ensure that if Mr. Lukic is giving evidence he begins that evidence with at least 25 hours of your time remaining; and if that's the case, he'll be giving evidence not next week but the following week.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you -- have you got that clearly in your mind that that is the situation you may be facing?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There's a lot of things clear on our mind and a lot of things on our palette.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As long as we know that you're aware of the situation. And therefore, you will have to indicate fairly soon whether or not he is going to give evidence. That is something you have to make a decision about. There are also certain points that I hope you can clarify about your latest witness notification, that's the one covering the period of two months; and if you can't answer today then the answer can be sent to us tomorrow. You have named on your latest list a witness Radovan Zlatkovic. He does not appear on your Rule 65 ter list, but your Rule 65 ter list includes two Radovan Zdravkovics. Now, we would like to know whether one of them is, in fact, Radovan Zlatkovic; and if so, which one. And secondly, you have listed as Zoran Amplic, is it Alimpic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Alimpic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I think I can address the first one. The gentleman that is -- that is on our notification is Zlatkovic, the name -- probably I think both of them had similar positions in Djakovica so there's always a little confusion with similar names, similar positions, but I'm working off the top of my head on that, but I do know that Zlatkovic is the one that made it on this most current list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But we need to know which of the wrongly designed Zdravkovics he is so that we can see what his evidence is going to be about and how he fits into the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Radovan's not -- oh, I see what you mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He's got to relate to the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Supplement the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And since there's two with the same name on the existing list, we don't know which is which.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct, we will have to do a supplement for the 65 ter with leave of Your Honours of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that should be clarified tomorrow if it can't be done just now. You also have a witness Pantic, Momir Pantic on your latest list -- sorry, in your 65 ter list, but on your list of witnesses for the next two months Pantovic, are they the same person?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's my understanding that's the same person since I'm not aware of a Pantovic on our 65 ter list nor on our supplement, and while I'm on my feet about the supplement I don't know if it was communicated but there has been that outstanding issue about the PJP commanders that we just recently got information about. I believe it's been communicated that we will be dropping all but I think one or two of those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've made it clear that you're dropping a number, that you're leading one, and that leaves one unclear and you should have received an inquiry about that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have, as I said, one or two, and we will react to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And there is another outstanding issue in relation to your recent notification, but I don't think I need to trouble you with it because these things are hopefully going to become clearer within the next three weeks. And that leaves just one other thing that I have noted, Mr. Ivetic, but I just want to be clear at this moment that I'm not misunderstanding anything about your position. You made a motion on the 11th of February objecting to the trial sitting schedule and asking us to amend it, and a decision on that was issued on the 20th of February. And in that decision on the 20th of February we drew attention to a remark that had been made in the motion itself, which depending perhaps on how you interpret it, others might say perhaps not, might have constituted a comment that wasn't exactly appropriate. And we did indicate that you ought to consider whether that comment should be withdrawn or remain. Now, there's been no response from you to that. Do we take it from that that you have made a deliberate decision to take no action?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I know that Branko Lukic and I talked about this, and quite honestly, Your Honours, in every motion that we file we carefully think out everything that we say and that particular passage was meant to highlight the very strong feelings that we had and the strong desire to ensure that these proceedings stay within the bounds of justice. And it was not meant as a -- as a criticism or as a -- as an accusation. Given that regard, we have to stand up for the rights of our accused, and I think the particular section I believe cited to the Statute and the Rules and several principles that apply to at least several national jurisdictions that I am familiar with. So in all fair conscience I believe professionally I cannot withdraw that comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And for the avoidance of doubt the comment was: "Surely the trial proceedings themselves are of more substantial value than simply being a mere legal formality to be endured before a judgement is rendered particularly" --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Along with one other section I believe, if I'm -- if I'm remembering correctly, there was a citation to Article 12 in the Celebici trial not being against the -- it's being called up. That is the -- that is -- that is the section and it does cite to Article 12 I believe of the -- in particularly in light of the requirement of the presumption of innocence. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- as complaint about the Trial Chamber. You know, sometimes things get interpreted differently in the heat of the moment, and if I was taken that way I apologise for that misconstruction or misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we take note of all that's been said on the various matters raised with us. As indicated last week, we are not in a position to take definite decisions without consulting with Judge Kamenova in the light of her review of the record of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What we anticipate is issuing an order next week once we've had that consultation and setting out a timetable and dealing with any other issues that need to be dealt with at that stage for the purpose of ensuring that we deal with the remaining stages of the trial as fairly and efficiently as I hope we've been able to deal with the trial so far. Tomorrow we are here at 9.00, and that session is until 1.45. So we now adjourn until tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 5th day of March, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24
